articles.title: Bank fraud victims want Ottawa to make big banks pay more
articles.summary: Every year, Canadians lose hundreds of millions to bank fraud — and are often left footing the bill. Now, customers of TD, Royal Bank, Scotiabank, CIBC and the Bank of Montreal are calling on Ottawa…

image.caption: Dozens of bank fraud victims, some who've lost their life savings, ask why banks aren't held more liable for losses. (CBC)

blocks.text: Over 10 months, Ralph Moore lost $450,000 to an online investment scam — drawn in, in May 2025, by a deepfake video of Prime Minister Mark Carney, heralding a new government investment platform where people could safely grow their savings.
The 88-year-old did transactions online and made multiple trips to his local TD Bank to arrange transfers, bank drafts and payments to other people's credit cards.
Now, Moore and his family are asking why the bank didn't do more to stop the transactions — and won't reimburse him.
"I don't think they protected me," he told Go Public from his home in Qualicum Beach, B.C.
His daughter Leslie Herrndorf, who lives in another city, says she was incredulous when she learned what happened.

items: Got a story you want investigated? Contact Erica and the Go Public team gopublic@cbc.ca

blocks.text: "How could $450,000 be allowed to be given away by a bank who'd been dealing with my dad for decades?" she asked. "They knew this was unusual behaviour."
Shortly after discovering the bank fraud, Herrndorf had her father's mental capacity tested. He failed.
When Ralph Moore tallied up the money he'd withdrawn from TD Bank, it totalled more than $450,000. (Mike McArthur/CBC)

Early on, the bank recognized that Moore was falling victim to a scam. It took some steps — questioning several of Moore's transactions and warning him and his wife about scams. It also alerted its fraud and anti-scam teams and at one point placed temporary restrictions on his account.

But Herrndorf wonders why the transactions weren't permanently blocked, her father's account frozen, or why the bank didn't make an effort to reach out to its client's adult children or possibly contact the police.

They are among the more than three dozen victims of bank fraud contacted by Go Public for this story who want to know: why doesn't Ottawa hold banks more liable for fraud, like some other countries do?
"It is outrageous, with the known number of frauds happening, that a bank has decided that this is the level of customer service that's acceptable," said Herrndorf.
Moore's daughter Leslie Herrndorf only learned her father was the victim of bank fraud when it was too late. Her father, a longtime TD Bank customer, had lost $450,000. (Michael McArthur/CBC)

Bank fraud is a massive and growing problem, according to the government's Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre. It reports people lost more than $700 million to all fraud in 2025 — and estimates only five per cent of victims report when it happens. Banking-specific numbers were not available.
Go Public receives emails almost daily from people who've suffered fraud losses: from e-transfer fraud to the bank impersonator scam to investment scams and credit card fraud.

items: TD Bank holds customer responsible for $15K loss, won't say how account hacking ruled out
New tuition scam left woman with $37K in fraudulent charges — and no help from bank, police or school
RBC and CIBC allow 89-year-old to drain life savings, lose $1.7M to scammers

blocks.text: In almost all cases, financial institutions hold their customers accountable – issuing similarly worded denial letters, in which people are accused of sharing passwords and account information or blamed for co-operating with scammers posing as investment experts, bank employees or other authorities.

"These are not negligent people, not stupid people," said Alexandre Plourde, a lawyer and analyst at Option consommateurs, a Montreal consumer advocacy organization that also regularly hears from bank fraud victims.
"I don't think the law does enough to protect consumers."
Go Public requested interviews with TD, Royal Bank, the Bank of Montreal, Scotiabank and CIBC after submitting inquiries about various customer losses at all five banks. All declined.

items: See statements from the big five banks

blocks.text: In February 2026, after Moore had lost virtually all of his money, TD shut down his account.
In a letter to Herrndorf written July 31, 2026, TD said it decided to "exit the client relationship" to "prevent further financial harm."

In a written statement to Go Public, a TD spokesperson did not answer any questions about Moore's case, citing client confidentiality. He said that protecting customers "remains a top priority through robust security, monitoring and education resources" and encouraged victims of fraud and scams to file reports with authorities.
'Zero responsibility'

Scotiabank customer Karla Zwicker says hackers stole over $13,000 from her accounts and line of credit last year. The bank said there was no evidence her account was compromised and declined to reimburse her.
"They've got to stop blaming the customers," said Zwicker, of Edmonton. "We need the government to do more."

Ivanka Bubic believed she was co-operating with RBC's fraud department last year, when scammers spoofed the bank's phone number and convinced her to withdraw money from her line of credit and approve charges on her credit card.
Moore was misled by a video like this that he saw online – a deepfake of Prime Minister Mark Carney, encouraging Canadians to invest in an online platform. (Michael McArthur/CBC)
RBC reimbursed its Montreal customer about $26,000 in credit card charges, but said she was responsible for $15,000 taken from her line of credit.
"It's crazy that they have zero responsibility when fraud happens," she said.

Deepak Kadaba of Mississauga, Ont., lost $3,400 to unauthorized withdrawals and debit transactions. BMO said the withdrawals were completed using his banking information, and the bank is therefore not liable.
"They're hanging customers out to dry," said Kadaba. "Where are the protections?"
'Big incentive' for Canadian banks
Cases like this often have very different outcomes in the U.K.
Since October 2024, the U.K. makes financial institutions shoulder the responsibility for fraud losses, except in cases of extreme negligence.
"The bank must reimburse consumers when they're a victim of fraud … unless the consumer has been grossly negligent," said Plourde, the lawyer. "That's a very high threshold for the banks to prove."
He says Moore's $450,000 loss is "unacceptable" and when customers are clearly being scammed, banks "should have protocols to go deeper, ask more questions."
Go Public requested interviews with TD, Royal Bank, the Bank of Montreal, Scotiabank and CIBC after submitting inquiries about various customer losses at all five banks. All declined. (CBC)
Other jurisdictions, like the E.U. and Australia, have also introduced laws that can force banks to reimburse fraud victims in many cases — though none have gone as far as the U.K.
"Putting more liability on Canadian banks would be a big incentive for banks to develop better security measures," said Plourde.

The Canadian Bankers Association, a trade group, told Go Public that "placing further liability on financial institutions alone will not prevent scams" and could "unintentionally have a negative impact" on bank customers and the economy.
Calls for liability laws
Consumer advocates like Plourde, some MPs and the Ombudsman for Banking Services and Investments have called on Ottawa to make the banks pay for fraud losses for several years.
But when the federal government introduced changes to the Bank Act on March 26, 2026, there was nothing about holding the banks responsible.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne recently told CBC News that he takes bank fraud seriously, and outlined several new measures the government is taking, including working on a national anti-fraud strategy.
"We're acting. We're not waiting, we're acting," said Champagne.
He did not commit to holding financial institutions accountable for fraud.

items: Rogers cutting telco customer service jobs amid complaints of long wait times
TD Bank holds customer responsible for $15K loss, won't say how account hacking ruled out
This Calgary woman won a $13K settlement — but says her paralegal kept the money

blocks.text: Meanwhile, a new survey released Oct. 13 by Option consommateurs found that Canadians overwhelmingly (87 per cent) believe that banks should reimburse victims of banking fraud, except when the customer has been grossly negligent.
The survey was conducted by Léger earlier this month, and involved just over 1,500 Canadians.
"The survey results show a public consensus on the need to strengthen banks' obligations," said Plourde.
"We're reaching record highs of fraud every year," he added. "It's time to act."

Banking on Fear: CBC Marketplace continues this investigation, seeing first-hand in the U.K. how British banks are now incentivized to stop fraud before it happens. Watch as the team confronts a scammer: Friday, Oct. 23 at 8 p.m. ET on CBC Television (8:30 p.m. NT) or stream anytime on CBC Gem and the official CBC Marketplace YouTube Channel

Go Public is an investigative news segment on CBC-TV, radio and the web.
We tell your stories, shed light on wrongdoing and hold the powers that be accountable.

If you have a story in the public interest, or if you're an insider with information, contact gopublic@cbc.ca with your name, contact information and a brief summary. All emails are confidential until you decide to Go Public.

articles.title: NATO's race against time: Senior commander warns alliance must adapt faster to deter Russia
articles.summary: NATO's supreme commander of transformation says the West's greatest vulnerability may not be a shortage of weapons, but the time it takes to build them — and the speed at which its adversaries are…

image.caption: NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Transformation Pierre Vandier says in a contest with Russia, the West’s greatest vulnerability may not be a shortage of weapons. It may be time. He spoke to CBC News recently during a trip to Ottawa. (Murray Brewster/CBC)

blocks.text: There's a nightmare that keeps one of NATO's most senior military commanders up at night and it's not what you might think.
It isn't the idea of Russian tanks rolling into the Baltic states or Poland. Nor is it a sudden military confrontation in the Arctic.

The scenario that keeps NATO Supreme Allied Commander Transformation Pierre Vandier up at night is the notion of the Western military alliance being caught unprepared and unable to keep up with the pace of technological innovation that's happening on the modern battlefield.
"Being late is really my nightmare," Vandier, a French admiral, told CBC News in an exclusive interview.

items: In Canada's drone-killing 'Sandbox,' companies compete for a $1M prize

blocks.text: "When I see people chatting, delaying some important decisions, not committing the money, using some … old-fashioned process, then it keeps me [up] at night."

Vandier met Chief of the Defence Staff Gen. Jennie Carignan and other high-ranking defence leaders for an up-close look at some of Canada's defence innovation plans during his recent low-key trip to Ottawa.
His warning about keeping pace comes at a particularly uncomfortable moment for the 32-member alliance.
'Being late is really my nightmare,' says NATO commander

Russia's war against Ukraine is approaching its fifth anniversary. Moscow has been accused of escalating a campaign of sabotage, cyberattacks and drone incursions in Europe along NATO's eastern flank. And Western governments are scrambling to rebuild military capabilities and defence industrial production lines that were allowed to shrink following the end of the Cold War more than three decades ago.
The danger, according to Vandier, is that the alliance is trying to prepare for tomorrow's war using institutions, procurement systems and assumptions inherited from yesterday.
"We thought that time was our friend," he said. "Now time is not our friend. It's the enemy's friend. The agenda is built on the other side."

During four years of grinding combat in Ukraine, Russia has suffered an enormous number of casualties. According to the British Ministry of Defence, as of mid-September, the Russian military has suffered 1.3 million casualties in the Ukraine war, including over 500,000 dead.

And there is a paradox at the heart of NATO's current security dilemma. While there have been devastating casualties and an enormous amount of equipment lost, the Russian Army that stumbled into Ukraine four years ago is not the same one on the battlefield today.
Vandier argued that Moscow has become more innovative, more adaptable and, in certain areas, more dangerous.
"The enemy is not the same as the one we had in 2022," he said.
"They learn, they adapt."
How NATO is flexing in the face of Russian aggression
He pointed specifically to Russia's evolving drone technology, including faster jet-powered attack drones that have complicated Ukraine's ability to defend its cities and critical infrastructure.
According to Vandier, the introduction of more advanced propulsion systems has significantly reduced the effectiveness of some Ukrainian drone-interception methods.

He estimated that interception success rates against certain Russian drones have fallen from approximately 90 per cent earlier this year to roughly 50 per cent as the technology has evolved. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, at the end of September, pegged the interception rate at about 55 per cent.

There's been a significant body of research published over the past year which challenges the assumption that Russia's enormous losses in Ukraine have left its military weaker, less capable or unable to threaten NATO.

Western military analysts increasingly describe a Russian military that has learned to adapt under fire, regenerate formations while fighting, absorb technological innovation and sustain operations despite staggering casualties.

items: How NATO is prepping in the Baltic skies for a possible confrontation with Russia
Putin appears to be eyeing NATO. The question is, will he actually attack?

blocks.text: "Russian military institutions reward loyalty over competence," said a study written last July by the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies, which argued Russia has become increasingly dependent on Chinese, Iranian and North Korean military assistance.
The authors argue that Russia's military can absorb new technology without developing the capacity to exploit it fully and effectively.

An assessment written last year by the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), based in the United Kingdom, was even more stark. It pointed to how Moscow is rebuilding equipment inventories, expanding units and reorganizing forces near NATO territory.
The think-tank's report said that Russia may restore important elements of its prewar ground-force equipment strength sooner than expected, although newly formed units could remain undermanned.

The IISS report also suggested that equipment shortages throughout the Russian military could potentially be resolved by late 2026 or early 2027. However, the full equipping and expansion of Russian ground forces could take until 2030 or 2035.
"It's a very fast-evolving environment," Vandier said.
Why 'grey zone' drone attacks are a problem for NATO

Russia has the ability to produce enormous quantities of relatively inexpensive drones and missiles. And that has exposed the limitations of Western defence industries designed to manufacture smaller numbers of highly sophisticated weapons.
Vandier believes the alliance has underestimated the scale of the challenge.
"The idea that the war is just a crisis of a few weeks is something that nobody can bet on anymore," he said.
He pointed to the enormous numbers of drones and missiles being employed in Ukraine as evidence that NATO must rethink not only what it buys, but how quickly it can replenish its arsenals.
The problem, Vandier said, is not simply a shortage of weapons. It is a shortage of industrial capacity.

Western economies have spent decades moving manufacturing and critical supply chains overseas, leaving defence industries dependent on materials and components that may not be readily available during a prolonged conflict.

items: Why Russia has Europe on edge
Norway PM 'prepared, but not afraid' of Russian incursion

blocks.text: Vandier challenged the suggestion that NATO's combined economic strength automatically translates into an overwhelming industrial advantage over Russia.
"I disagree with the point where we have a good industrial depth," he said.
"The challenge now is to produce what we can produce in mass and rapidly, and not only what we have on a very exquisite and limited quantities."
The implication of that is significant. In a prolonged conflict with Russia, the West would quickly run out of equipment and ammunition.
The U.S-Israeli war with Iran has seen a number of published reports about the scarcity of high-end weapons systems.
For Canada, Vandier's assessment comes as the federal government embarks on an unprecedented expansion of defence spending.
After decades of relatively limited investment, Ottawa has committed billions of additional dollars to modernizing the Canadian Armed Forces and rebuilding the country's defence industrial base.
Vandier said he has been struck by the scale of the change.
"It's very impressive to see how this country, which has spent a limited amount of money focused on NORAD, now is opening eyes on all the NATO [area of responsibility]," Vandier said.

articles.title: DPWH eyes November award of key Bataan-Cavite bridge section
articles.summary: The Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) aims to award a 3.1-kilometer section of the Bataan-Cavite Interlink Bridge (BCIB) by next month, subject to approval of the Asian Development Bank…
articles.byline: JON VIKTOR D. CABUENAS, GMA News

blocks.text: Published October 19, 2026 3:50pm

The Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) aims to award a 3.1-kilometer section of the Bataan-Cavite Interlink Bridge (BCIB) by next month, subject to approval of the Asian Development Bank (ADB), which is co-financing the project.

Based on the BCIB’s Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) uploaded on the DPWH website, the section set to be awarded next month is Package 6 of the BCIB, which involves the South Channel Bridges and Approaches.

“Mag-a-award kami ng (We will award the) P6, which is the most critical part of Bataan-Cavite, within November. It’s already pending with the ADB for concurrence,” DPWH Secretary Vivencio “Vince” Dizon told reporters on the sidelines of the EJAP Infrastructure Forum in Makati City.

Package 6, or the South Channel Bridge, will be located between Corregidor Island and Cavite, the bigger of the two proposed cable-stayed bridges. It will have a span of 1,800 meters between the two pylons, creating an opening for ships to pass through as they go in and out of Manila Bay.

It will also feature two monopole-style towers standing 346 meters above the seabed, or about 306 meters above sea level. It will likewise have a “Nearshore Navigation Channel” provided near the Cavite shoreline.
“‘Yung foundation kasi nung P6, ‘yung matataas na tore. Ang dalawang foundation na ‘yan na malalaki, igugulong. Each foundation is bigger than Araneta Coliseum, just as a trivia,” Dizon said.
(The foundation for P6 are the tall towers. The two massive foundations will be rolled out. Each foundation is bigger than the Araneta Coliseum, just as a trivia.)
The BCIB is planned as a 32-kilometer bridge connecting Mariveles in Bataan and Naic in Cavite, expected to cut travel time between the provinces from five and a half hours to 45 minutes.

The project is bankrolled through a multi-tranche financing scheme, under which the Asian Development Bank (ADB) will finance $ 2.1 billion, while the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) will co-finance $1.14 billion. —AOL, GMA News

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa

French president Emmanuel Macron has declined interior minister Laurent Nuñez’s offer to resign after widespread riots over the weekend, despite “failures in anticipation and intelligence” that were deemed to worsen the crisis engulfing the country.

Macron said Nuñez should stay to ‌ensure a chain of command is retained within the police and security forces, and has also asked Nuñez to set up ‌as quickly as possible new approaches to deal with looters, ​the Élysée Palace added, quoted by Reuters.
Macron has asked the minister to “put in place new operational methods for security forces” to get a grip over the crisis.
Saturday, one of the most violent days of unrest in years, left public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted and at least 2,400 people arrested in cities across the country.
In a TV interview on Monday, Nuñez admitted that the police “lost control” in some cities during the protests.

blocks.caption: Riots in central Paris over the weekend, with 2,400 people arrested nationally. Photograph: Poitout Florian/ABACA/Shutterstock

blocks.text: In an address to the nation last night, Macron criticised “unbridled violence”.
“Watching these images, we have all asked ourselves how could French people do this to France?” he said.
I will bring you more updates on this today.

Separately, I will also be keeping an eye on Ukraine, after another night of heavy attacks by Russia killing at least one and injuring eight people, and with conflicting reports about whether Kyiv authorities had been warned about the strikes.

I will bring you all the key updates here.
It’s Monday, 19 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

articles.title: Mother assessed as posing no immediate risk to others three weeks before Elizabeth Struhs’ manslaughter, inquest hears
articles.summary:
Queensland correctional services officer did not have access to details of Kerrie Struhs’ past offending which included child neglect

  • Get our

blocks.text: Elizabeth Struhs’ mother, Kerrie, was assessed by correctional services as being of no immediate risk to others by an officer who had no access to her offending history, three weeks before she and others caused her eight-year-old daughter to die, a Brisbane inquest has heard.

Kerrie Struhs was sentenced to five months’ jail for child neglect after failing to take Elizabeth to hospital to treat her type 1 diabetes in 2019. Coroner Ainslie Kirkegaard has previously heard that Elizabeth was so unwell when she presented at hospital that she was nearly dead, and was in a coma.
Elizabeth was discharged from hospital into the care of her father, Jason Struhs, by the department of child safety. Jason was later also convicted for child neglect over the 2019 incident.
When Kerrie was released from jail on 16 December 2021 on court-ordered parole, she was assessed by two different correctional officers, the inquest heard on Monday.
Elizabeth died just 22 days later of diabetic ketoacidosis, after Jason stopped providing insulin to treat her type 1 diabetes at their home in Toowoomba, Queensland.
Kerrie met with a parole intake officer the day of her release from prison in 2021.

That officer told the court that she didn’t have access to the QP9 for Kerrie’s conviction – a file produced by prosecutors and the police that would have included details about her offence – or the judge’s sentencing remarks.
She also had no other knowledge of Kerrie before the meeting, but was able to access some details online, including her offence type.
The court later heard that the other information was not accessible due to an administrative error.
The parole intake officer conducted an “immediate risk assessment” of Kerrie at the meeting.
The court was shown the file, which include the question: “Has the offender described any issues that may pose an immediate risk to themselves, others or impact on their immediate management?”
The officer marked this “no”.
A child safety officer had previously marked Elizabeth as “safe” just days after her 2019 admission to hospital.
The file containing the risk assessment also disclosed a conversation between Kerrie and the parole intake officer about her 2019 offence.

“Kerrie said she believed that God would heal the child but she wouldn’t interfere with someone else getting the child treatment …” the officer reported, in contemporaneous notes presented to the court.
“She said she would do the same again. She said that she would keep that trust in God that he would heal.”

Kerrie had previously made similar remarks to healthcare workers, child safety officers, police and others. Brisbane-based specialist doctors considered her beliefs so dangerous that Elizabeth could not safely live in the same home as her, but were overruled by child safety.
after newsletter promotion
A senior correctional services officer told the court Kerrie should have been flagged for the “serious offenders unit” due to causing “serious child harm”.
That would have led to additional oversight over her case, the officer said.

Kerrie’s parole intake officer told the court she upgraded her level of risk from “low” to “standard” due to the seriousness of her offence, which meant Kerrie would have to meet with a parole officer weekly.
She also booked her another in-person meeting with a different parole officer, on 23 December.
The officer who met her on 23 December said she met with Kerrie for just 10 or 15 minutes and didn’t take the same steps she might have at any other time of the year, two days before Christmas.
Both officers were duty officers, filling in for others.
Kerrie was also scheduled to meet with a parole officer a third time, on 6 January 2022.
Elizabeth died on 7 January after Jason withdrew her insulin from 3 January 2022.
Kerrie, Jason and the other 12 adult members of the religious sect they were members of were convicted of manslaughter over Elizabeth’s death last year.
None of the witnesses in the coronial inquest can be identified, for legal reasons.
The inquest continues.

Malacañang has named Vice Admiral Rommel Supangan as the new commandant of the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG), replacing retired Admiral Ronnie Gil Gavan.
During a press briefing on Monday, Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said Supangan was appointed by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
“Ngayong araw ay itinalaga ni Pangulong Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. si incoming PCG Commandant… Vice Admiral Rommel Supangan,” Castro said.
(Today, President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. appointed incoming PCG Commandant… Vice Admiral Rommel Supangan.)

“... Siya po ay papalit kay Admiral Ronnie Gil Gavan at magpapatuloy sa mandato ng Philippine Coast Guard na pangalagaan ang ating baybayin at siguruhin ang kaligtasan at seguridad sa ating mga nasasakupang karagatan. Congratulations po kay Vice Admiral Rommel Supangan,” she added.

(...He will replace Admiral Ronnie Gil Gavan and continue the mandate of the Philippine Coast Guard to safeguard our shores and ensure safety and security in our maritime domain. Congratulations to Vice Admiral Rommel Supangan.)
Supangan is a graduate of the Philippine Military Academy "Marilag" Class of 1995, according to the Palace.
In 2008, he earned his master's degree in Maritime Affairs, majoring in Marine Environment and Ocean Management, from the World Maritime University in Sweden.
Before his appointment as PCG Commandant, Supangan served as commander of the Marine Environmental Protection Command from February 2026 to October 2026.

During his service in the Coast Guard, he also served as commander of the Coast Guard Fleet from June 2025 to October 2026 and as acting director of the Coast Guard Strategic Studies and International Affairs Center from June 2025 to February 2026.

Supangan is also a recipient of the PMA Cavalier Award for Coast Guard Operations (Senior Officer Category), as well as the Coast Guard District Palawan Award with Commandant PCG Unit citation and streamer.
On Monday, Marcos led the PCG Change of Command and Retirement Ceremony of Gavan at South Harbor in Port Area, Manila.
Appointed exactly three years ago in 2023, Gavan served as the 30th commandant of the PCG. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: France hit by debt sell-off as protests unnerve investors
articles.summary: After Macron condemned ‘unbridled violence’, difference between French and German 10-year borrowing costs widens

blocks.text: France was hit by a fresh wave of selling in its bond and stock markets on Monday after violent protests over the weekend left public buildings burned, hundreds of shops looted and thousands of arrests across the country.
Almost 2,400 people have been arrested in France, the interior ministry said on Sunday, with police deploying teargas in confrontations with protesters.
The French president, Emmanuel Macron, condemned the “unbridled violence” in a televised address on Sunday night.
“Looking at these images, we all asked ourselves: what is going through their minds? How can French people do this to France?” he said.
The chaos has spooked investors in France’s government debt, with the yield on its 10-year yield rising by seven basis points to 4.849%. Yields rise when prices fall.
This widened the difference between the French and German 10-year borrowing costs – which is a metric for the risk premium attached to French debt.
Meanwhile, the two-year yield rose by 2.5 basis points to 3.571%.
Violence erupted across the country after weeks of peaceful demonstrations over conditions in schools and the cost of living.

While tens of thousands of people have attended peaceful marches to demand more teachers and repairs to decrepit schools, different groups have clashed with police in cities including Paris, Bordeaux, Nice and Marseille.
Jim Reid of Deutsche Bank said the protests “won’t make it easy for the international community to be totally comfortable buying OATs [French government bonds]”.
He said: “With France already facing a difficult fiscal backdrop and the 2027 election approaching, the weekend adds another layer of political risk for markets.”
The 30-year bond, which is a benchmark for the French government’s long-term cost of borrowing, rose by three basis points to 5.397%.
after newsletter promotion
The rise in borrowing costs will add further strain to France’s public finances, as the government also tries to pass a budget for next year to rein in its deficit.
France’s debt-to-GDP stood at 1115.6% in 2025, while its budget deficit was 5.1%, compared with 94.3% and 4.3% for the UK respectively.

The French government is preparing a budget that would involve cutting pensions spending and funding for government departments, excluding defence. However, there are growing fears that political pressure could derail these plans, which could push up borrowing and add more to the country’s debt pile.
The euro also slipped slightly against the US dollar, down by 0.13% in early trading on Monday, falling to $1.122.
The French Cac 40, which tracks the biggest companies listed in Paris, fell by 1% at the start of trading in Paris, compared with a 0.4% drop on the pan-European Stoxx Europe 600 index.

articles.title: DA seeks P62-B El Niño mitigation plan
articles.summary: The Department of Agriculture (DA) said on Monday that it was proposing a P61.99-billion action plan to mitigate the impact of El Niño on the country"s food supply and livelihoods.

blocks.text: Published October 19, 2026 3:31pm
The Department of Agriculture (DA) said on Monday that it was proposing a P61.99-billion action plan to mitigate the impact of El Niño on the country’s food supply and livelihoods.
In a statement, the DA said the proposed interventions aim to minimize agricultural production losses and help farmers and fisherfolk cope with the effects of the climate phenomenon.

“We need to plan ahead and ensure farmers have the support they need to cope with a potentially severe El Niño, including access to drought-tolerant rice varieties and other appropriate inputs,” Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. said.
“Early preparation is crucial to minimizing production losses and protecting farmers’ livelihoods and the country’s food supply,” he added.
The proposed spending package includes P6.2 billion already released under the government’s Unified Package for Livelihoods, Industry, Food, and Transport (UPLIFT) Program, the DA said.
However, the department noted that P371 million worth of proposed interventions remained unfunded.
These include cloud seeding operations (CSOs) and measures to manage infestations of red-striped soft scale insect (RSSI), which affects sugarcane production, the DA said.

The department also plans to coordinate with other government agencies on additional El Niño interventions. These include a cash-for-work program with the Department of Social Welfare and Development and the Trabahong-Dagat and Blue Enterprise Development Program with the Department of Labor and Employment.

The DA said it has begun releasing fuel subsidies to fisherfolk, while the distribution of subsidies to farmers using mechanized equipment is targeted to begin in the last week of October or in November.— MCG, GMA News

MANILA, Philippines – Gasoline prices are set for a substantial rollback starting Tuesday, October 20, although diesel prices will rise again as global fuel markets continue to face supply disruptions.
The Department of Energy (DOE) announced the following permitted price adjustments for October 20 to 26:

items: Gasoline – rollback of at least P4.30 per liter
Diesel – increase of up to P2.60 per liter
Kerosene – rollback of at least P1 per liter

blocks.text: This moves opposite of last week’s adjustments, when gasoline prices increased by P1.56 per liter and kerosene by P1.77, while diesel dropped by P3.01 per liter.
The latest gasoline rollback comes amid improving availability in Asian markets. China has resumed refined petroleum product exports following a brief suspension earlier in October.

Diesel, however, continues to face tighter global supplies, with inventories remaining low even as governments move to release emergency stocks. Higher freight costs have also added pressure to diesel prices.
The DOE said global fuel prices remain affected by developments in the Middle East, where attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure continue to threaten oil supply.

Local pump prices also remain well above levels seen before fighting involving Iran and US-Israeli forces broke out on February 28. In the last full week before the conflict, DOE data showed common retail prices in Metro Manila at P56 per liter for gasoline RON95, P54.70 per liter for gasoline RON91, P55 per liter for diesel, and P83.47 per liter for kerosene.

The Philippines is a net importer of petroleum products, making local pump prices vulnerable to global oil price swings, foreign exchange movements, regional refined fuel prices, and disruptions in international supply routes.

Separately, excise taxes on liquefied petroleum gas and kerosene remain suspended under Executive Order No. 125, issued by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in September. The tax relief does not cover gasoline or diesel. – Rappler.com

articles.title: UK government promises disabled air passengers better safeguards
articles.summary:
Despite recent progress, almost a fifth of air travellers with disabilities are still dissatisfied with their experience

Disabled passengers will have better safeguards when flying, the…

blocks.text: Disabled passengers will have better safeguards when flying, the government has pledged, including protection from damaged wheelchairs and support from trained staff.

A report from an industry-led accessibility group said there was “much more to be done” but progress was being made, a year after a review led by Tanni Grey-Thompson demanded action to improve air travel in response to numerous incidents in which passengers had been left stranded without assistance.

The Department for Transport said airports had added more staff training and a new standardised system has been set up to prepare airlines for handling mobility aids, after more than 1,000 wheelchairs were damaged in transit in 2024, equivalent to more than 80 a month.
Almost one in five disabled passengers are still dissatisfied with their air travel experience though, according to an industry body, and requests for assistance are continuing to rise.

The government is planning to remove the maximum payout in compensation for lost and damaged wheelchairs, and to give the aviation regulator new powers to fine airlines and airports when passengers are not given the assistance they need to travel.
The changes are expected to be in the civil aviation bill which is progressing through parliament and which the government said would give air passengers stronger protection and consumer rights.

The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, said: “People must be able to fly with dignity and peace of mind. For disabled passengers this means not worrying about their wheelchair coming back in one piece, or whether staff will be there to support them around the airport.
“We’ve backed industry to overhaul staff training, prevent damage to mobility aids and create easy, simple ways for passengers to share key information before they fly.”

The co-chairs of the aviation accessibility implementation group, which is assessing progress on the 19 recommendations in Grey-Thompson’s report, said: “There is much more to be done, but we have made a positive start. We will be focusing now on embedding more of the changes that are needed to enable disabled people to fly with confidence and dignity.”
after newsletter promotion
The chief executive of lobby group Airlines UK, Tim Alderslade, said the number of passengers requiring assistance was up nearly 10% year on year.
“82% report that they are satisfied with their air travel experience which demonstrates the efforts and progress airlines are making for those who require additional support when they fly,” he said.

articles.title: Lazaro summons China ambassador Jing, says it’s not his place to taunt PH officials
articles.summary: President Marcos had earlier said a discussion was to be had between himself and Beijing's envoy

blocks.text: SUMMON. DFA Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro summons Chinese ambassador Jing Quan on October 19, days after he made a barely-veiled threat against the Philippines in a media interview.
DFA
President Marcos had earlier said a discussion was to be had between himself and Beijing's envoy

items: Philippine Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro summoned Chinese ambassador Jing Quan after his provocative remarks about China's military presence in the region.
Lazaro emphasized the importance of diplomatic dialogue and criticized Jing's statements as undermining bilateral relations, while the DFA expressed commitment to constructive engagement with China.
The situation has led to calls from Philippine politicians for Jing's expulsion, highlighting ongoing tensions over maritime disputes in the South China Sea.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines — Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro summoned on Monday, October 19, Chinese ambassador Jing Quan days after Beijing’s envoy said Manila should be “fortunate” that China does not use force in its disputes.

“Secretary Lazaro told the Ambassador that the statement was provocative and unacceptable, and does not contribute to creating understanding. She stressed that such language aggravates an already sensitive bilateral atmosphere and undermines the shared efforts of both countries to build mutual understanding and cooperation,” read part of a Department of Foreign Affairs statement.

In an interview with media, Jing reacted to Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr.’s statement that it was Beijing and not Manila that was a troublemaker in the region. After speaking about the importance of dialogue and cooperation, Jing said: “We should feel fortunate enough that you have a neighbor like China in this region. If we want to use force, we may easily win. But no, we’ll not use force. We love peace.”

blocks.caption: Marcos to summon China envoy over use of force ‘threat’

blocks.text: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., in a chance interview on October 16, said Jing’s remarks “deserves a discussion between the ambassador and myself” when asked if he would summon the envoy.

It is unclear yet why Marcos decided not to summon Jing himself — although there had been a sentiment, even within the DFA, that it would be best for Lazaro to summon the ambassador instead. Jing was only recently summoned by Marcos — in July 2026, also over remarks made in a media interview.

blocks.caption: DFA MEETING. China ambassador to Manila Jing Quan is summoned by Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro on October 19, 2026.

blocks.text: “It is not the place of a foreign mission to publicly criticize or taunt Philippine officials and legislators who are acting within their mandates. As a democracy, the Philippines values freedom of expression and a plurality of voices, and it will not accept attempts by a foreign envoy to intimidate those who exercise them,” said the DFA of Jing and Lazaro’s meeting.

Lazaro, according to the media release, “emphasized that sensitive issues are best addressed through established diplomatic channels and bilateral mechanisms, which preserve space for dialogue and engagement.”

“The Department remains committed to candid dialogue and constructive engagement, in line with its mandate and the direction of the President. It will keep open lines of communication with China and work to stabilize bilateral relations, especially in non-sensitive areas, while firmly upholding the country’s consistent positions on important issues,” said the DFA.

Over the weekend, Philippine politicians have criticized Jing and the embassy, with some even calling for his expulsion or declaration as persona non grata. Only the President can expel a diplomat assigned to the Philippines.
In response, the embassy has dared legislators to push through with this calls — again, even if it’s only Marcos who can make such a declaration.
“The Department reserves the right to take further diplomatic action as it deems necessary,” the DFA said, without giving specifics.
Lazaro was joined by DFA’s senior leaders in her meeting with Jing.

In a briefing on October 19, Palace Undersecretary Claire Castro said Marcos valued “diplomacy” especially in defending its rights, entitlements, and interests in the West Philippine Sea. She did, however, concede that the embassy’s latest statements were seemingly no longer diplomatic.

The Chinese embassy in Manila has amped up its rhetoric since Jing took over in December 2025. The embassy, through its spokesperson, have constantly been engaging in online word wars with spokespersons and officials of the Philippine government.

Maritime rows are at the center of tensions between Manila and Beijing. China claims almost all of the South China Sea, including an area Manila calls the West Philippine Sea. For Filipino maritime frontliners, China’s claims mean having to deal with harassment and even harm out at sea.
Beijing does not recognize the landmark 2016 Arbitral Award, which validated the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone and deemed Beijing’s supposed historical claim invalid. – Rappler.com

articles.title: 3 in 5 schools still without security guards despite campus shootings
articles.summary: The Department of Education is asking the Senate for an additional P8.18 billion in its 2027 budget to hire security guards and install metal detectors and perimeter fences in public schools,…

blocks.text: October 19, 2026 | 2:45pm
DepEd seeks P8.18B more for security

MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Education is asking the Senate for an additional P8.18 billion in its 2027 budget to hire security guards and install metal detectors and perimeter fences in public schools, following three deadly school shootings since June.

About 39% of DepEd schools have security guards as of October 11, according to the agency’s safe school environment audit, which it presented at a Senate budget hearing on October 16. That leaves roughly three in five schools without one. DepEd’s presentation did not say how many guards are currently deployed.

Meanwhile, fewer than half of DepEd schools, or 48%, had active CCTV cameras, and about one in five lack a perimeter fence. Functional metal detectors are in 51% of schools, an improvement from June, when the detectors were only in 11% of schools, according to DepEd data.

The proposed 2027 budget in its current version sets aside just P500 million for school security guards, enough to hire 1,667. Testifying before a Senate finance subcommittee last week, Education Secretary Sonny Angara said the agency was seeking money "for security guards, for metal detectors, for perimeter fences… which were not really included in the budget previously."

Of the P8.18 billion, DepEd is seeking P4.55 billion to hire 15,155 more guards, P2.13 billion for metal detectors and walk-through scanners, and P1.5 billion for perimeter fences, according to its presentation to the panel.
DepEd's own figures put the cost of a guard at roughly P300,000 a year. At that rate, the request would fund about nine times as many guards as the budget bill currently covers.

Campus security has moved up DepEd's priorities after shootings at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City on June 22, at Ateneo de Zamboanga on August 18 and at Banga National High School in South Cotabato on September 18.
DepEd has since issued Order No. 006, series of 2026, which tightens campus security and gadget control, sets proportional sanctions for students and simplifies how cases are reported and referred.
The request for additional funds for security and equipment is part of a P147.93-billion wish list that DepEd hopes to add to its 2027 allocation.
Under the House-approved General Appropriations Bill, DepEd and its attached agencies would receive a total of P969.79 billion, which is P45.52 billion, or 4.48%, less than this year.
Angara, however, conceded that getting the full amount on its wishlist was "medyo suntok sa buwan (a bit of a long shot)."

Sen. Bam Aquino, chair of the Senate basic education committee who presided over DepEd's budget hearing on October 16, said senators shared the goal of bringing education spending back to 4% of gross domestic product, despite many "competing interests" for public funds.
Angara noted that 4% is only the floor and that UNESCO recommends 4 to 6%.

DepEd had been caught off guard by the presence of "nihilistic violent groups" manipulating students, Angara admitted during the hearing. He said officials first learned about them only after the Tacloban shooting. "We didn't realize how wide they were, how organized they were," he said.

The DepEd chief also admitted the agency was unprepared for the aftermath as some of its personnel had not been trained to respond to campus violence of this scale. "After Tacloban alone, on the first day, there were 400 people who needed psychological first aid," Angara said.
Aquino urged DepEd to prioritize which schools need security equipment more than other smaller campuses.

Aquino urged DepEd to identify which schools need security equipment most, rather than aim to cover every campus. Large schools clearly need CCTV, he said, but some schools outside city centers have perhaps 200 students. In those areas, “the need for a CCTV is not as much,” and a security guard may not be necessary, he said.

The senator asked DepEd to list the specific schools that need CCTV, metal detectors, perimeter fences and guards, and to show how far it is from covering them, before the proposed 2027 budget reaches plenary debate.

CJP leaders remain in custody, magistrate alleges threat to life
The release ofCockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, who were sent to five days of judicial custody on October 14 for entering Jantar Mantar, has been delayed.
Jantar Mantar has been a prominent protest site in the heart of Delhi for decades. However, Delhi police blocked it amid heavy barricading and deployment.

The duo's judicial custody was supposed to end on Sunday, but their bail hearing was stalled after the special executive magistrate failed to arrive at the scheduled time and later recused himself, citing a threat to his life.
The Delhi Police have registered a case against unknown persons for threatening the magistrate in connection with Ranka and Das's bails.
According to The Times of India, police sources said the magistrate is being pressured to release Ranka and Das without delay.

articles.title: In Bacolod, one MassKara group chose to dance with the hard truths
articles.summary: Despite not winning the competition, one group's artistic expression gets praised for addressing societal issues, while the festival itself served as a platform for showcasing Bacolod's resilience…

blocks.text: CONTROVERSIAL. A giant billboard used as a prop by the Barangay 13 contingent draws attention during the MassKara street and arena dance competition in Bacolod on Sunday, October 18. The billboard highlights corruption, a flood-control scandal and other issues.
Ambo Delilan/Rappler

Despite not winning the competition, one group's artistic expression gets praised for addressing societal issues, while the festival itself served as a platform for showcasing Bacolod's resilience and creativity

items: Barangay 13's performance at the MassKara Festival highlighted the struggles of Bacolod City, including corruption, inflation, and public service failures, contrasting with the festival's usual celebratory themes.
The performance, directed by Chloe Jan Lorca Gavin and Edrian Conde, aimed to showcase the realities faced by residents rather than insult public officials, emphasizing resilience in adversity.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

NEGROS OCCIDENTAL, Philippines – Bacolod City’s Barangay 13 did not win the MassKara Festival’s grand street and arena dance competition on Sunday, October 18. But as the other groups competed for prizes, its dancers brought something less comfortable to the celebration: a portrait of a city struggling with corruption issues, rising prices, a power crisis and failing public services.

The group was the only one among eight barangay contingents to build its performance around the problems facing Bacolodnons, projecting those realities on a giant billboard as dancers moved before thousands of spectators at SM City Bacolod. The performance also reached many viewers watching online from elsewhere in the Philippines and abroad.

Its presentation was a departure from the festival’s familiar display of colorful costumes, elaborate props and choreographed smiles, serving as a reminder that behind Bacolod’s reputation as the “City of Smiles” are people facing crises that do not disappear when the music starts.

blocks.caption: THE CHAMPIONS. Barangay Taculing dancers perform their routines en route to winning the barangay category of this year’s MassKara Festival street and arena dance competition. The contingent takes home the P1 million cash prize. Ambo Delilan/Rappler

blocks.text: Under the direction of Chloe Jan Lorca Gavin and Edrian Conde, Barangay 13’s performers brought Bacolod’s troubles to the MassKara stage: systemic corruption, a flood-control scandal, inflation, power shortages across the Visayas, poor water services, drug addiction and other health concerns.

The presentation came amid mounting public scrutiny of P300 million in Tourism Infrastructure and Enterprise Zone Authority projects, an unfinished probe into alleged P5 billion in flood-control projects, and P6.1 billion in loans incurred under two past city administrations.

blocks.caption: Bacolod’s P300M TIEZA projects face scrutiny over delays, defects at cultural landmarks

blocks.text: Bacolod, the capital of Negros Occidental, is also seeing a red-striped soft scale insect (RSSI) infestation that has damaged about 2,000 hectares of sugarcane farms across 10 rural barangays, causing estimated losses of more than P200 million.

The city was placed under a state of calamity on August 5. On October 10 and 11, the Department of Social Welfare and Development’s Negros Island Region office provided P10,325 each to 2,957 affected sugarcane farmers and laborers through its Emergency Cash Transfer program.
Conde said the group did not intend to insult public officials watching from the stage or turn its performance into a political statement – it merely wanted to show what residents were experiencing.
“We only showed what is happening in our area, and that is our concept of love for victory,” he said in Hiligaynon in an interview with Rappler on Monday, October 19.
Conde added: “Amon man ginpakita nga ang kadalag-an indi lang makita sa mga medalya kundi makita taman ko paano ‘ta atubangun ang mga problema.”
(We also showed that victory is not only seen in medals, but also in how we face problems.)
The performance, he said, moved from ugly realities toward a more hopeful conclusion. In that lay the festival’s central idea: resilience in the face of adversity.

blocks.caption: ‘Ti, ano kung Benitez ka?’: Bacolod allies nearly come to blows over city’s debts

blocks.text: Wilson Gamboa Jr., convener of the Amlig Tublig and Amlig Kuryente groups, said Barangay 13’s artistic concept and design deserved respect.
“They just communicated the ideas about society, civic identity and political and economic circumstances in Bacolod,” Gamboa said.
He said the performance was about escaping harsh realities and celebrating hope and resilience.
“So, nothing wrong with that candid artistry,” he said.
Another, Christian John Weber, said Barangay 13’s performance echoed the call to address national and local issues affecting Bacolodnons.
“Its theme, indeed, needs to be appreciated and respected,” Weber said.

But at the end of the day, it was the group from Taculing which won the MassKara Festival street and arena dance competition in the barangay category and bagged the top prize, followed by Mandalagan and Handumanan as first and second runners-up, respectively.

Mandalagan Elementary School and Bacolod City National High School won in the school category at their respective levels, while the group from Barangay Tangub topped the Electric MassKara float parade.

With Bacolodnons and many worldwide watching the street dancing at the SM City grounds and online, Bacolod Mayor Greg Gasataya said MassKara had turned into a world-renowned festival, turning tragedy into resilience and, ultimately, revelry.

Gasataya said MassKara serves as a compass for Bacolodnons as they confront various challenges and crises. He said the festival allows them to showcase their resilience to the Philippines and the world.

The three-day festivities featured the Electric MassKara float parade on October 16, followed by street and arena dance competitions for school and barangay contingents on October 17 and 18, respectively.
Colorful floats, costumes, headdresses and props showcased Bacolod artisans’ creativity, while the street and arena performances made MassKara more than a celebration.
Wallace Minn-Gann Chow, representative of the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office (TECO) in the Philippines, said he was amazed by the performances in the barangay category.
“This is my first time to witness MassKara, and I find it very amazing,” he told Rappler.
Chow and his wife, Samantha Tai, were among the top guests at the MassKara street and arena dance competitions on October 17 and 18.
MassKara was coined from the English word mass or a multitude of people, and the Spanish word cara, meaning face.

Started 46 years ago amid two major crises – the near-collapse of the Negros sugar industry and the MV Don Juan sea tragedy between Mindoro and Romblon, which claimed roughly 180 lives – the festival’s origins echo the challenges Bacolod faces today. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Brazil: Lula, Bolsonaro clash in heated presidential debate
articles.summary: The candidates traded barbs, including over Bolsonaro's ties to US President Donald Trump in their first debate, days before the October 25 election runoff.

image.caption: In a tense moment, Lula challenged Bolsonaro for both of them to open their personal finances to scrutinyImage: Jean Carniel/REUTERS

blocks.text: Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and populist Senator Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday had a heated exchange during their first face-to-face presidential debate.
The televised debate, which saw the candidates trade insults and accusations, came a week before the October 25 presidential runoff.
Bolsonaro finished nearly two points ahead of Lula in the election's first round earlier this month.
How did the presidential debate turn heated?
The contentious debate focused on the economy, public security, corruption and Brazil's relations with the United States, before it devolved into personal attacks.
Bolsonaro criticized Lula over the cost of living, public security and social spending, accusing him of spending recklessly to secure re-election.
Lula called Bolsonaro "a habitual liar, a thug," alluding to his alleged ties to Rio de Janeiro's paramilitary groups.
"Lying is ​the Bolsonaro family's strong suit," Lula said.
Bolsonaro retaliated by accusing Lula of being tainted by corruption, saying during the debate that it was better he maintains a distance "because my wallet could be stolen."
"Brazil is going to retire you," Bolsonaro told Lula.
Meanwhile, Lula also brought up the populist Senator's ties to US President Donald Trump.
"It is striking how the Bolsonaro family is subservient to American interests," said Lula, accusing Bolsonaro of conspiring to "hand over" Brazil's rare earth minerals to the US.

Flavio's father also came up during the discussion. Former President Jair Bolsonaro is currently serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest over a coup attempt after his failed 2022 re-election bid.
The next presidential debate is scheduled for Friday, October 23.

blocks.caption: Brazilian politics have been increasingly polarized for nearly a decadeImage: Miguel Schincariol/AFP

blocks.text: Thousands rally in support
Meanwhile, tens of thousands of supporters of both candidates rallied in cities across Brazil ahead of the debate, flooding the streets of Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and other cities.
In Sao Paulo, Bolsonaro's supporters called for the release of Jair Bolsonaro.
On the other hand, at Rio's Copacabana Beach, Lula supporters led a "rally for democracy." There were similar events in Brasilia and 16 other state capitals.

articles.title: Funding shortages force World Food Programme to cut aid to Gaza
articles.summary: The number of people helped by the UN agency in the Palestinian territory will drop by about a third - from 1.6 million to 1.1 million.

blocks.text: Dalal al-Dahdouh said the WFP food handouts her family received were insufficient even before the cuts
ByYolande Knell
Middle East correspondentReporting fromJerusalem

One of the main suppliers of food aid to the Gaza Strip, the World Food Programme (WFP), says that it is being forced to "drastically reduce lifesaving assistance" to the Palestinian territory due to funding shortages.
Overall, the number of people helped by the UN agency will drop by about a third - from 1.6 million to 1.1 million.
The cuts will hit as winter approaches and at a time when many families in Gaza are still struggling to feed themselves.
One effect is that the number of hot meals that are currently being provided by community kitchens will be cut from 250,000 to 150,000 each day.
Families living in hard-to-reach areas, for example near the so-called Yellow Line, which demarcates Israel's area of military control, will receive a meal every other day instead of daily.
Nearly all of Gaza's 2.1 million population remains displaced and two-thirds rely on food aid to survive.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Mervat al-Satari, a mother-of-five, says the cuts are a "disaster"

blocks.text: Mervat al-Satari, a mother-of-five, says the cuts are a "disaster"

"It's a disaster! What will we do with these reduced rations? How will we provide for the little ones?" said Mervat al-Satari, a displaced Palestinian mother-of-five at a camp in the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis after being told of the WFP's news. "Sometimes we wait for these meals to eat."

"This will affect us a lot. The daily aid was somehow ticking the box but now it will be every two days," said Sawsan Bahloul, who is also from al-Mawasi and is a mother of three. She added that the portions given by the community kitchen - usually pasta or lentils with occasional potatoes and aubergines - were already too small to feed her family.
The Palestine director for the WFP, Shaun Hughes, is clear that the cuts are being made because of finances, and "not because the needs are coming down, or because we don't have access - we do."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Nearly all of Gaza's 2.1 million people are displaced, with many living in camps like those in al-Mawasi

blocks.text: Nearly all of Gaza's 2.1 million people are displaced, with many living in camps like those in al-Mawasi

Already, since July, there have been reductions in cash transfers provided to some half a million people, meaning they have less money to buy food in local markets. The number of Gazans given bags of flour and ration boxes by the WFP will now fall from 1.1 million to 600,000 each month.

The WFP received less than half as much funding for its Palestinian operations in 2026 as in previous years. The agency says it urgently needs $450m (£338m) to maintain "critical" operations over the next six months.
Despite a ceasefire between Hamas and Israel that was agreed a year ago, humanitarian conditions in Gaza remain dire.

There has been no reconstruction and little recovery, with Israel tightly controlling the entry of goods through crossings. While food markets are now well stocked, few can afford to buy from them. More than 80% of people in Gaza are unemployed so most of the population relies on aid.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Two-thirds of the population relies on food aid to survive, according to UN-backed experts

blocks.text: Two-thirds of the population relies on food aid to survive, according to UN-backed experts
Families currently receiving the WFP food handouts complained to the BBC that already these were insufficient and gave them little diversity in their diets.

"The flour isn't enough and the food boxes aren't enough either," said Dalal al-Dahdouh, who is living in the ruins of her home in Gaza City with her family of eight. She fears the new cuts will have "a major impact".

The mother draws a contrast between the current desperate situation and life before the war. "In the past, thank God, we had our own home and a wonderful life. We had fresh vegetables, proper sanitation facilities and our own land," she said. "Now we live entirely on aid, including WFP vouchers."

There is no cooking gas available in Gaza because the Israeli government considers it a "dual use" item that could be used by Hamas for military purposes. Wood is expensive, so many families send their children into the street to find plastic and cardboard to burn as fuel to make bread or heat food.

"It's still a very concerning humanitarian situation, people living in brutal conditions, most people still without a proper home, living in tents, poor access to water and sanitation and healthcare," Hughes of the WFP told the BBC. "Cuts to food assistance are going to compound that hardship that families have been facing for three years now."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Families, including Sawsan Bahloul's, are forced to burn plastic and cardboard as fuel for cooking

blocks.text: Families, including Sawsan Bahloul's, are forced to burn plastic and cardboard as fuel for cooking
Humanitarian workers say that despite a modest improvement in Gaza compared to a year ago, acute food insecurity and the risk of famine returning continue to loom over the territory.

In July, the Integrated Phase Classification (IPC) - the world's foremost experts on food security - reported that two-thirds of the population - 1.4 million people - were "expected to face crisis or worse levels of acute food insecurity in July-December 2026".

For now, the WFP says it can continue supporting bakeries that provide one-third of Gaza's bread needs and provide nutritional assistance to about 300,000 women and children. It also delivers health food snacks to some 200,000 children.
In the occupied West Bank, the WFP is continuing to give assistance to some 200,000 Palestinians, having halved the number of recipients in September.
The agency says food insecurity is rising in the territory mostly due to increased Israeli settler violence and Palestinian displacement.

articles.title: What Earth's sixth mass extinction event means for humans
articles.summary: Human activity is driving plants and animals to extinction at an unprecedented rate. As countries meet in Armenia to discuss ways to reverse nature loss, DW reveals how declining biodiversity is…

image.caption: From tiny bees to big whales, all of the players on nature's team are essentialImage: Yonhap News/IMAGO

blocks.text: From the tiniest microbes in the human gut to giant whales in the ocean, biodiversity is the sum of all life on the planet. It's another word for nature. And because nature is like a team, every player has a job.

When various species from trees to animals work together, they regulate weather, maintain soil health, purify water and support food production. These benefits are known as ecosystem services and they underpin human wellbeing.

"It is really an abstract concept, but we experience it absolutely every day," said Rebecca Shaw, chief scientist at conservation group WWF "And we almost never think about it when nature is functioning."

blocks.caption: Without biodiversity, the variety of food humans eat would not be available. Declining biodiversity is endangering crop productionImage: Burak Kara/Getty Images

blocks.text: But as it declines, she and other scientists are calling on the world to really think about it. Because biodiversity is struggling as humans push ecosystems to the brink through intensive farming, burning fossil fuels,and pollution from sources like plastic and chemicals.

Over the past 52 years, monitored vertebrate populations have collapsed by an average of 73%, while freshwater ecosystems are faring worst with a drop of 85%, according to WWF's recent Living Planet report.
It tallies with other studies that show a million animal and plant species face extinction unless humanity reduces its pressure on nature.

"It is a really steep decline," said Shaw. "What it's telling us is that nature is in trouble, and it's an early warning indicator of the fabric of life that we depend on for freshwater and food and for clean air is unravelling."

blocks.caption: Deforestation directly drives biodiversity decline because forests are home to more than 80% of all land-based speciesImage: Juancho Torres/AA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Thousands of policymakers, business leaders and civil society groups are meeting in Yerevan, Armenia over the next two weeks for COP17, the latest UN biodiversity summit, to advance commitments to reverse nature loss by 2030. But progress towards those targets remains insufficient, with funding and implementation among the biggest challenges.
What happens when ecosystem services decline or disappear?

Take wetlands as an example. Some 85% of these vital ecosystems disappeared between 1700 and 2000. One study from Canada's University of Waterloo found that habitats like marshes and swamps in Southern Ontario provide C$4.2 billion (€2.63 billion) worth of water filtration services each year, removing nutrients like phosphorus and keeping drinking water sources clean.
The study found that as they disappear, water quality worsens, which massively increases the cost of treating it.
Another example is the decline in pollinators like bees and bats. More than 75% of global food crop types rely in part on animal pollination.
Why climate change is driving species loss

At the same time, soil and ecosystem degradation coupled with storms and heat waves linked to climate change are already damaging harvests. A recent UK government report stated that every critical ecosystem is on a "pathway to collapse," warning that nature's decline posed a grave threat to global food supply and geopolitical stability.

"The UK, like many other countries, relies on imports for much of the food and so is reliant on ecosystems around the world," said Louise McRae, a research fellow at the Zoological Society of London, who also contributed to WWF's Living Planet report. "This is why we need to care about global biodiversity."
It also provides the basis for many modern human medicines, with some 50% coming from natural compounds.

blocks.caption: Poisonous frogs could be a source for new medications but as species disappear we could be missing out on novel drugsImage: Al Carrera/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: Penicillin, the first antibiotic, is produced by a mold and is estimated to have saved over 500 million lives. Before its discovery, a person could die from a simple cut. Around 70% of cancer drugs come from natural products or synthetic compounds "inspired by nature," according to the World Health Organisation (WHO).
As biodiversity disappears, humans risk losing access to undiscovered treatments.
Does it really matter if one species disappears?

To return to the "nature as a team" metaphor, if a player disappears, sometimes a species with similar functions in the ecosystem can jump in as a substitute. But not always, particularly if it's a "keystone species." They play a disproportionately large role in their environments, and their disappearance has significant knock-on effects.
The oyster is one such species. Wild oyster populations are facing massive declines, while 85% of their reefs have been lost worldwide. An adult oyster filters up to 50 gallons of water a day.

"No one would ever think, they did anything but sit in a shell and be slimy," said Shaw. "But you lose oysters, you can lose water filtration and clean water, you can lose the habitat for many other species that we interact with or sometimes consume."

blocks.caption: People around the world rely on oysters and other marine life for their livelihoods and as a food source. Oysters are also a keystone speciesImage: Misper Apawu/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: And, said Shaw, the humble oyster protects coastal communities from storm surges. If you lose it "you lose the coastal protection."

The loss of a single species can also lead to more disease. One study suggests a decline in red foxes in North America is linked to the spread of Lyme disease, a tick-borne illness that also impacts humans.
Is humanity living through a sixth mass extinction and is it too late to prevent it?

The planet has experienced five mass extinctions when a large proportion of species globally disappeared over a short geological period. Extinction is a natural process. But the rate at which species are disappearing today, suggests Earth is experiencing a sixth event, driven largely by human activity, according to scientists.
Both McRae and Shaw called the declines extremely worrying, but said they shouldn't provoke despair.

Though she acknowledges that the underlying global trend is moving in the wrong direction and cannot be ignored, McRae says "the statistics are there to just motivate us to action rather than to cause alarm."
And the Living Planet report also highlights conservation successes, showing that nature can recover.

The number of green sea turtles, for example, had fallen significantly, but has now bounced back. This is thanks to a massive worldwide effort to protect nesting beaches and changes to fishing practices that reduce accidental capture.

blocks.caption: Since sea otters on the North American Pacific Coast have rebounded, so too have kelp forestsImage: Malcolm Schuyl/FLPA/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: Sea otters are another example. Prized for their fur, in the 1800s they were hunted to near extinction on the US Pacific Coast. When they disappeared, it meant sea urchins had no predators, leaving them free to decimate kelp forests.

That matters because as well as providing habitat for other species, these giant underwater groves protect coastlines from storm surges and absorb carbon, making them important for climate protection.
Following a ban on commercial hunting, sea otters have also rebounded, helping kelp forests recover.

"You can see that ripple effect that really had an obvious and a measurable impact. But critically, it can be reversed," said McRae, adding that biodiversity loss and climate change are intertwined and exacerbate each other but have joint solutions.
"We're learning how to turn things around at very small scales," said Shaw. "Now the real challenge is to turn things around at very big scale so we can see it in the global indicators."
Baltic seagrass: restoring a secret climate ally
