articles.title: Trump defends Russia sanctions waivers, accuses Zelenskyy of 'prolonging war'
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump again accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war. The remarks come amid renewed tensions over US policy toward Moscow including waiving…

image.caption: Trump (right) repeated his claim that Ukraine was targeting Russian refineries to hurt Republicans ahead of the US midterm election [FILE: September 22, 2026]Image: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: US President Donald Trumpon Sunday defended his decision to waive some sanctions on Russia, accusing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war.

"My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don't want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

"Zelenskyy doesn't care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him, and that Crooked Joe Biden gave him in the past, he doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did," he added.
Trump signed an executive order late Friday waiving broad new sanctions mandated by legislation named for the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, a staunch supporter of Ukraine's defense.
He has also temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel, allowing supplies to flow into global markets in a bid to lower fuel prices ahead of US midterm elections on November 3.
Trump links Russia sanctions waiver to fuel prices ahead of midterms
Opinion polls suggest that Republicans could face significant losses in the election, as voters voice growing frustration over fuel prices that have surged since the Iran war began in late February.
Most economists believe the suspension of congressionally approved sanctions on Russia and the diesel deal with the Kremlin will do little to lower US fuel prices.
Trump also repeated his claim that Ukraine was targeting Russian refineries to hurt Republicans ahead of the midterm election.
How Trump is helping Putin
The move drew a sharp response from Kyiv and its allies, further straining relations between Trump and Zelenskyy.
Zelenskyy warns Ukraine cannot prevail if US backs Russia
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Sunday that Ukraine would lose its defensive battle against Russia if the United States switched sides and supported Moscow.
"If the United States will take the side of Russia, of course we will not prevail," Zelenskyy told NBC's 'Meet the Press' calling a withdrawal of US support "a historic mistake and big tragedy."
He said Washington had resumed sharing intelligence after it was "blocked for some period of time," adding that Ukraine had missed critical intelligence on ballistic missile attacks for three days.
Zelenskyy also criticized US restrictions affecting Ukraine's war effort, saying, "We are strategic partners," but "we cannot applaud when someone turns against Ukraine."
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended Trump's suspension of new sanctions on Russia, saying Trump wanted to assess their impact on the global and US economies.
Zelenskyy speaks to US envoys as Trump renews criticism

Volodymyr Zelenskyy spoke to US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner as Russia and Ukraine attacked each other's energy infrastructure, leaving thousands without power in Ukraine and setting an oil refinery ablaze near Saint Petersburg.

After the talks, Zelenskyy said "a lot depends" on the US position, adding that "this war must be brought to an end." Ukraine was ready to work "constructively" and "honestly," he said, calling for the same approach from its European and US partners.
Zelenskyy said he also discussed deliveries of US Patriot air defense systems as Kyiv struggles to counter Russian missiles.
A US-led push to end the war has yet to yield a breakthrough, with Trump expressing frustration at both Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Zelenskyy accused Moscow of violating Trump's "energy ceasefire" 76 times and warned Russia planned to deprive Ukrainians of heat and electricity before winter. Russian strikes left "tens of thousands" without power, he said, while Ukrainian officials reported three deaths.
Ukraine launched drones at Putin's hometown of Saint Petersburg late Sunday, setting an oil refinery ablaze and killing one person, Moscow said.

articles.title: Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia
articles.summary: Two men tell of the work they say they have been doing to support Ukrainian intelligence during the war.

blocks.text: Two Russian men secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services have given rare accounts of operations they claim to have been involved with, that have targeted military assets and personnel inside Russia.
One of the men, whom we are calling Ivan, claims to have played a role from Russia in Ukrainian drone attacks on strategic bombers and munitions factories on his home soil.
He features in a BBC World Service documentary about the shadowy world of Russian saboteurs.
The documentary, by independent Polish journalist Marcin Mamon, also features a man we are calling Foma, a Russian living in exile in Poland.

Foma runs a network of undercover volunteers in Russia, that surveils high-level officers that the GUR - Ukraine's military intelligence service - is considering targeting, he says. He stresses they are never involved in the attacks themselves.

He was also tight-lipped about who they were surveilling, but after Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was assassinated in December last year in Moscow, Foma admitted he had provided the Ukrainians with intelligence on him.
There have been previous media reports of Russian sabotage groups, but it is rare to get access to someone operating on the ground, like Ivan, explaining alleged activities.

The GUR has confirmed that Ivan and Foma are both working for the agency. But it also has acknowledged that it cannot know the full picture. When Ivan's handler was pressed on whether he could be trusted, the handler replied: "I'm not sure of anyone, except myself."
And both the GUR and the men are cautious about how much detail they share, making it impossible to verify the activities the men claim to have carried out.

The broad tactics Ivan and Foma describe, however, have been acknowledged by the Ukrainian authorities. Kyiv has spoken of its strategy of co-ordinated drone attacks on what it claims are legitimate targets inside Russia, and has acknowledged it uses secret agents for this.

There have also been several political assassinations in Russia since the start of the war. As a matter of policy, Ukraine never officially admits or claims responsibility for targeted attacks, though a Ukrainian intelligence officer has previously admitted to the BBC it was behind the killing of senior military figure Lt Gen Igor Kirillov in December 2024.
It is difficult to confirm how many Russians are doing this kind of work for Ukraine. According to Foma, they number about 300-500, though this is impossible to verify.

items: If you are outside the UK, watch on YouTube, external and listen to the BBC World Service Documentary Podcast - Shadowmen: Russians working with Ukraine

blocks.text: Ivan and Foma say they are both opposed not just to Russia's war in Ukraine, but to President Vladimir Putin's regime - and believe his political future depends on the war's outcome.
"At the moment... I think the [Putin] regime might fall if they lose the war… Through our actions... we are trying to speed this up," Ivan says.
His work, he told Mamon, involved surveilling military sites, and locating places to hide drone components, in preparation for potential attacks on Russian assets.
"When these [drone] components are combined… it turns out a formidable weapon, which with a single blow can destroy an object that costs many, many millions of dollars," Ivan said.
He sent Mamon a video which showed him apparently hiding explosives near a Russian military airfield.
If he had been caught, he would have been charged with terrorism, and jailed for decades.

Foma's work is different - he operates remotely, training his volunteers in Russia, online. Mamon watched him conducting one such tutorial - on how to trail a senior military official marked for surveillance.

"You will get a file... from me or a colleague… with the proposed target. The file will contain [the target's] photo, his data, his details, date of birth, age, and a description of him. There'll be information on his car, if he has one. When you go to the target, don't take a phone," he told his volunteers.
Foma was once part of the Russian elite, so he claims to have a unique set of contacts and constant flow of insider information.
He showed Mamon on his laptop how he mapped military targets.
"This shows a database... the location of storage warehouses, and military units. Where generals live… Where the pilots of strategic bombers who shell Ukraine live.
"In order to break the system, you need to understand how it works. Then you can aim for their weak points."

He said there were about "three dozen" people in his network split between Russia, Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe, with the contingent outside Russia providing logistical support, such as tracking targets' digital footprints.
Foma stressed that the GUR suggests the targets to be surveilled, but that he and his team check for themselves that these individuals should be considered military criminals.
"As a rule… we also check the data [on that person]… Only after that we say whether we work or not."
But he argued that his team's actions were justified.
"I want people who do terrible things on behalf of Putin and Russia in Ukraine… to understand that they'll have to pay for it. I want them to get scared."
Foma stressed that he only passed on intelligence to the Ukrainians, and his network did not carry out any assassinations themselves.

Of the assassination of Gen Sarvarov, killed in December 2025, he later texted Mamon to say: "Keeping track of him took quite an effort. He lived alternately with his mistress and his colleague. Covered his tracks and constantly changed his schedule."
But Foma did not share any plans with Mamon and the BBC in advance.
Ivan, however, was tight-lipped about the work he had been involved with, even after the event.
Foma did his own digging on Ivan.

After checking with his military intelligence contacts in both Ukraine and Russia, he thought it likely that Ivan had been involved in a plan to strike Russia's largest military drone factory at Yelabuga in June last year, external. One person was reported to have been killed in the incident.
Ivan stressed that the aim is always to try to avoid harming civilians.
Operations have clearly been risky for Ivan too.
"The most serious case was when my car was stopped for inspection and I had the handmade explosives on me. The risk was very high - however as you can see, I was not detected," he said.
To mitigate the risk of being compromised, "there is no clear structure" to the work, he said, adding he had never met and did not know the identity of others he had been working alongside.
Foma has the same rule for his operatives.
"As soon as you start gathering people in groups, in general chats… leaving a mark on the internet, with a high probability this whole group will be quickly detained or destroyed," he said.
Ivan stressed there were few people left in Russia suitable for this kind of work.
"Most of the ideological people have either left the country or are already behind bars," he said.

Many Russians involved in sabotage work on their native soil are therefore either oblivious - for example lorry drivers unaware that their cargoes have been compromised - or are individuals who have been paid, the BBC understands.

Ivan, on the other hand, says he is doing this work for ideological reasons - he used to be a member of the political opposition. As such, his movements would be expected to be monitored closely by the Russian authorities.
So it was a surprise that he managed to frequently leave Russia and return.
Mamon persuaded Ivan to drive him into the Georgian desert, where they could speak freely - and asked him how the Ukrainians could trust him.
"You go to a third country… where [Ukraine's] agents meet you… and conduct lie detector tests," Ivan told him.

Mamon asked Ivan to put him in touch with one of his GUR handlers in Ukraine. This man immediately rang Ivan on speaker phone - apparently demonstrating that Ivan worked for him. They spoke in code, referring to "repairs at the school".
But later, the handler admitted he could not rule out the possibility Ivan might work for the Russians too, either voluntarily or under duress.
Foma thinks the fact that Ivan can travel freely does not necessarily constitute a red flag.

"There are all sorts of holes in [the country's governance], and if you know them, or are just lucky, then you can jump through the holes… and live in the system. Like a mouse in a piece of cheese," he told Mamon.

Perhaps more compellingly, if Ivan had also been spying for FSB, it would seem likely that he would share what he knew of Ukraine's attack plans with the Russian agency. More than a year before a devastating strike by more than 100 Ukrainian drones, Ivan had been telling Marcin there would be a major attack on strategic bombers on military airfields across Russia, though he never said when or where.
Marcin asked Ivan how he coped with the work.
"Fear is always present," he said. "It follows me everywhere. Even if you don't do anything, you're still afraid. This is Russia."
But he was optimistic that eventually his life would change.
"Putin won't live forever," he said.

articles.title: Outrage after Meta suspends No Kings Instagram account during protests
articles.summary:
‘Meta owes us an explanation,’ group says as organizers fear censorship after account goes dark for several hours

The coalition leaders behind nationwide pro-democracy protests that have…

blocks.text: The coalition leaders behind nationwide pro-democracy protests that have drawn millions of Americans to the streets in recent years were frustrated when its Instagram account was temporarily shut down during its latest demonstration on Saturday.
The No Kings movement’s account went dark for several hours while protests focused on increasing early voter turnout were underway, sparking censorship fears.
Meta apologized on Saturday and blamed the account’s temporary suspension on an automated action that’s triggered “when accounts post, share or comment at very high frequencies”.
“Unfortunately, that automated action was clearly taken in error,” Meta spokesperson Andy Stone, wrote on X. “Everything is now working as it should and we sincerely apologize.”

“We have regained access to our accounts, but Meta still owes us an explanation,” the No Kings Coalition posted on their Instagram page, on Sunday. “Restricting communications about voting in the middle of an election is unacceptable.”
In a longer statement, Stone cited the “high volume” of reading profiles, posts and hashtags in “intense bursts” on Saturday caused their AI tool to detect the activity as automated bot traffic.

“This activity caused our automated protections to incorrectly take the No Kings Instagram account offline. An automated re-review of the removal action an hour later recognized that shouldn’t have happened and restored the account,” Stone said. “It unfortunately took additional time for us to straighten out the situation with admin access to the IG account. We want to reiterate our sincere apology for the error.”
Organizers remained skeptical about Meta’s explanation that high-frequency posting triggered an automated response, and said members “posted only a handful of times and livestreamed to thousands”.
Senator Bernie Sanders also expressed concerns on Sunday, on X, saying that “billionaire ownership of the media” had resulted in the suspension of the No Kings account.

Connecticut senator Chris Murphy called for an investigation into the incident in his own social media post, saying it was an indictment of Meta’s “outsized influence” on US culture and politics. “How were they not ready for the biggest day of anti-Trump protest of the campaign?” Murphy said. “An investigation is warranted, at the very least, to understand why Meta (which effectively functions these days as a private government) was unable to protect protest against Trump, while it spends so much time trying to get close to Trump.”

Despite the technical blip, hundreds of planned events continued. At the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, a band played for a few hundred people in caps and coats, many of whom were dancing and held signs saying “VOTE EARLY” and “HANDS OFF MY VOTE!”
In Atlanta, city councilman Michael Julian Bond told the crowd: “The constitution gives you one power, right? That is the power to vote. Are you gonna use that power?”

On the streets of downtown Los Angeles, protesters carried umbrellas to protect them from the sweltering heat and a band trailed behind them on a rolling stage, the New York Times reported; the crowds cheered calls for abolishing ICE and passing California’s billionaire tax.

The No Kings movement began last summer, in response to a broad set of concerns about federal layoffs, immigration enforcement and foreign wars. The demonstrations have continued to tackle a wide range of issues, and typically lean into anti-Trump fervor.

This year’s focus on voting ahead of the midterm elections is in part due to the supreme court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act, as well as fears about Trump once again sowing chaos by baselessly calling election results into question.

No Kings organizers said they planned to recruit volunteers at Saturday’s events to mobilize in case of “election sabotage”, Leah Greenberg, a co-executive director of Indivisible, a progressive group that helps organize No Kings events, previously told the Guardian.

articles.title: Obama condemns comments by ‘border czar’ that Ilhan Omar could ‘of course’ be denaturalized
articles.summary:
Ex-president urges Americans to defend congresswoman, saying ‘there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her’

Former US president Barack Obama condemned comments by Donald Trump’s…
articles.byline: José Olivares and Sanya Mansoor in New York

blocks.text: Former US president Barack Obama condemned comments by Donald Trump’s “border czar” that the Republican presidential administration could “of course” strip Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar of her citizenship and deport her.
Obama wrote Sunday morning, on X, that “the full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president.”

He urged all Americans to defend Omar, regardless of their political beliefs, adding: “if this becomes the new normal, there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her – or that future presidents, in either party, won’t do the same.” Obama, too, has had his citizenship scrutinized by Trump, who more than a decade ago fueled false conspiracy theories that Obama was born in Kenya and therefore not eligible to be president.
Tom Homan, Trump’s “border czar”, was asked on Saturday by a Fox News host whether the investigation into Omar could involve “denaturalizing and then deporting her”, Homan answered: “Of course”.
“If you lie during the naturalization process, there is a process to denaturalize somebody,” Homan said. “We’ve done it before. It’s a long, tedious process, but it’s been done before.
“And certainly, if the evidence points that way, that could happen.”

Homan’s comments were the first remarks explicitly mentioning denaturalization and deportation in connection with Omar that were attributed by name to a top Trump administration official since federal agents raided the Minnesota US House representative’s home on 12 October.

The search of Omar’s home sparked major backlash and accusations that the Trump administration was weaponizing the federal government to target a political rival whom the president and his supporters have openly fantasized about denaturalizing and deporting.

The federal government’s investigation into the most prominent Somali American in the US is to see whether Omar or her family violated any laws when obtaining her citizenship. The investigation was launched only weeks before the November midterm elections, in which Omar is on the ballot.
Homan also seemed to imply during his Fox News appearance that the federal government is investigating Omar for other allegations – but refused to give details.
“I’m not going to go there,” Homan said. “I know things, but that’s a question for the FBI.”

Omar – a naturalized US citizen from Somalia – was a child when her father filled out the immigration paperwork which the federal government is evidently scrutinizing. Her father, Nur Omar Mohamed, died in June 2020.

blocks.caption: Tom Homan applauds as Donald Trump speaks at a rally in Syracuse, New York, on 9 October.  Photograph: Mandel Ngan/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Obama stated in his post on X that Omar arrived in the US with her father when she was 12, and five years later, when her father became a naturalized citizen, she became one, too, because she was 17. (An 18-year-old would have had to apply for citizenship separately, he noted.)

“Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen,” he wrote. “Federal agents have raided her home, confiscated personal records, and seized her phone – all to try and uncover a nonexistent smoking gun from 20 years ago that will somehow make their case.”
In a letter after her home was searched, Omar’s attorneys accused the US justice department of potentially influencing an election in violation of longstanding internal policy.

The move to investigate Omar came amid a heightened offensive by the administration in pursuit of its aggressive anti-immigrant crackdown. In addition to funneling resources and deploying droves of officials to arrest, detain and deport undocumented immigrants throughout the country, the administration has also escalated its on offensive on legal migration.
The administration has been pursuing dozens of cases nationwide in which they are attempting to denaturalize Americans born outside of the US, who they claim fraudulently obtained their citizenship.
As Homan alluded to on Sunday, the lengthy denaturalization process requires a federal investigation and drawn-out court proceedings.
after newsletter promotion
Nonetheless, as of April, the US justice department had reportedly identified nearly 400 foreign-born citizens that it sought to investigate.

The investigation into Omar follows unsubstantiated accusations by rightwing figures who support Trump that she obtained her citizenship fraudulently. Omar denies the accusations, which also include allegations that her ex-husband is her brother, whom she only married so he could obtain immigration status in the US.
The federal government reportedly seized Omar’s phone during the raid on her home and has issued more than a dozen subpoenas, including of Omar’s relatives.
Omar’s attorneys have demanded that the federal government return her property and preserve any audio or video taken during the search.

Omar has said she and her family fled Somalia’s civil war when she was eight and spent years in a refugee camp in Kenya. She and her family came to the US in the 1990s, and she became a naturalized US citizen in 2000, according to her lawyers.
There is “no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status”, said her attorneys’ letter, which was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

Even veterans at the Department of Justice expressed shock over the targeting of Omar, according to reporting by NBC News. “I was astounded to see a search of a sitting congressperson this close to an election,” said Peter Carr, a former career justice department spokesperson, NBC News reported.

“Historically, the department has been very adamant that politics plays no role in investigative decisions they make and they try very hard to avoid taking overt actions that might even have the perception of influencing an election.”
After the raid on her home, Omar posted on X that she was “ok”.

“Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar also wrote. She said: “Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns” for years – and “this is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.”
“I will not be silenced,” Omar added.

articles.title: EU tariffs aimed at China hitting Ukraine, steel boss says
articles.summary: The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies says the country has been "bundled together" in measures aimed at curbing cheap imports.

blocks.text: The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies has called on the European Union to drop import restrictions on products made from the country, arguing it has been "bundled together" in measures aimed a curbing cheap imports from the likes of China.

Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, told the BBC the recently-imposed tariffs on imported steel to the EU were "unfair" and had been put in place "without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in".
He said he wished to see "at least a carve out" for Ukraine to access the EU market.
A spokesperson for the European Commission said the EU "took into account the difficult situation" of Ukraine when deciding its steel policy.
The trading bloc has recently imposed restrictions on steel imports in an effort to protect steel manufacturers of member nations.
It has capped the amount of steel which can enter the EU tax free at 18.3 million tonnes per year - a 47% reduction from 2024 levels.

There are some country-specific quotas in the policy, but the overall aim is to cut the amount of steel that can be imported due to member nations struggling to compete with cheap imports from the likes of China and Turkey.
Despite a free-trade agreement (FTA) being in place between the EU and Ukraine, the FTA does not stop the EU from introducing separate trade protection measures.
"Ukraine has been bundled together into those measures without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in," Ryzhenkov said, pointing to the war with Russia.
"Access to the European market is crucial for survival," he added. "The restrictive measures that have been put in place by the authorities in the European Union, they don't help.
"I think it's unfair that Ukraine has been treated in the same way as all of the other importers into the European Union."
The Ukraine steel industry estimates steel exports to the EU could ultimately fall by about 50–60%.
The EU said Ukraine's specific steel quota guaranteed exports of the metal, but acknowledged this was at a "level lower than in the past years".
"Despite the war effort, Ukraine remains an important exporter of steel to the EU," a spokesperson said, adding it had "offered compensations" to its largest suppliers, which included Ukraine.

Steel products are a foundation in Ukraine's economy. Before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's national income and a third of its exports. The EU is its top customer.
But the industry has suffered from the continued Russian bombardment.
All of Ukraine's steel mills have been bombed at points since the conflict began in 2022, but Ryzhenkov said strikes had "intensified significantly recently".
At one point in September, there was "no single tonne of steel produced" in Ukraine for the first time in about 150 years, he added.
Almost 800 Metinvest workers have been killed since the war began.
Ryzhenkov said the company had "improved the covered areas" at its mills where workers can shelter during air raids.
"The only thing we can do is to design procedures to keep people safe and just obey those procedures and try to minimise the risks."
"Unfortunately, you cannot cover a whole steel mill to avoid it being damaged."
Ryzhenkov said he expected the coming winter to be "one of the hardest in our history".
"We are in a dire situation when we don't have logistics to access any other market apart from the EU and cutting our available market by 60%, that doesn't help for the industry to survive."

articles.title: ‘Champi’ may re-intensify into super typhoon, to enter PAR Tuesday
articles.summary: Typhoon Champi has weakened as it moved west-northwestward over the sea west of Guam, but may re-intensify into a super typhoon.

blocks.text: October 19, 2026 | 7:15am
Satellite rendering shows Typhoon Champi taken on Oct. 18, 2026.
PAGASA via Facebook
MANILA, Philippines — Typhoon Champi has weakened as it moved west-northwestward over the sea west of Guam, but may re-intensify into a super typhoon, PAGASA said Sunday night.
In its 11 p.m. bulletin on Sunday, October 18, the state weather bureau said Champi was carrying maximum sustained winds of 175 kilometers per hour near the center, with gusts of up to 215 kph.
It is moving west-northwestward at 15 kph.
The center of Champi was estimated at 1,830 kilometers east of Southeastern Luzon, outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR).
Champi is expected to enter the PAR by Tuesday morning or early afternoon. Once inside the country's monitoring area, it will be given the domestic name Rosal.
Strong winds, rainfall
PAGASA said tropical cyclone wind signals may be raised over the northern and eastern portions of Northern Luzon and parts of the Bicol Region as early as Monday evening or Tuesday morning.
The highest wind signal in the current forecast scenario is Signal No. 3 or 4.
Gusty conditions may affect most parts of Luzon and the Visayas, as well as portions of Mindanao, beginning Wednesday.
The tropical cyclone is also expected to bring heavy rainfall to Extreme Northern Luzon.
Sea conditions
Moderate to rough seas may begin affecting the northern and eastern seaboards of Luzon and the eastern seaboards of the Visayas and Mindanao by Tuesday.
Hazardous sea conditions, with very rough to very high seas, may affect the northern and eastern seaboards of Luzon from Wednesday onward.
PAGASA said a gale warning for very rough seas will be issued on Tuesday evening or Wednesday morning.
Track, intensity
Champi will continue moving west-northwestward until it enters the PAR on Tuesday, after which it is expected to move toward Taiwan while remaining over the Philippine Sea.
The tropical cyclone is forecast to maintain its strength over the next 12 hours before re-intensifying beginning Sunday evening or Tuesday.
PAGASA said Champi may again reach super typhoon category, with further intensification possible while it moves over the Philippine Sea.
A gradual weakening trend is expected to begin on Wednesday after the tropical cyclone reaches its peak intensity.

articles.title: Trump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going
articles.summary: The US president blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table.

"I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said on his Truth Social messaging platform, adding that he didn't want to "do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table".
Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky deepened.
Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday that siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake".

Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev has responded to Trump's order by calling it "an important and truly historic moment", and saying the sanctions would have inflicted "serious damage" on the US and global market.
Trump also claimed in his Truth Social post that Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did", adding "he could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now".
Zelensky has pushed for an end to fighting, and has repeatedly said that Putin doesn't want peace, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week. Ukraine has accused the Trump administration of withdrawing key military support.
Since then, Zelensky declared it was nice to be among "real leaders" while addressing a European Union summit, after Trump said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Putin.

articles.title: Ebola: Kenya cases rise to 8, spreads to 8th Congo province
articles.summary: A senior health official in Kenya said there have now been 8 Ebola infections in the country, while in DR Congo the disease has spread to an eighth province.

image.caption: Kenya has been on heightened alert due to a major Ebola outbreak in Central Africa [FILE: October 7, 2026]Image: Andrew Kasuku/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Kenya's Health Ministry on Sunday confirmed another case of Ebola, bringing the number of confirmed infections in the country to eight.
News of another patient in the East African state came as health officials in Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) reported that the outbreak there had spread to an eighth province.
What Kenya's health director general said
"Today, 38 people were tested, and one tested positive for Ebola," Health Ministry Director-General Dr. Patrick Amoth said in an ​interview on Kenya's Citizen TV.
"He is a 49-year-old man ​who is not a healthcare worker. He developed ​fever, headache and muscle pain," Amoth said.
He went on to explain that the latest case was a patient attendant who cleaned utensils and linen and had likely been exposed to Kenya's first Ebola case, discovered earlier this month.
Amoth said patients in quarantine were being tested after developing symptoms and that the other six patients were stable after receiving supportive treatment. The first patient died on October 5.
Kenya has been on a heightened state of alert as a major outbreak of the highly contagious disease spread in Congo in central Africa.
Ebola now in 8th province in Congo
Also on Sunday, authorities in DRC said that the Ebola outbreak had spread to an eighth province in the north.
Congo's Health Ministry said that two cases including a death were recorded in Nord-Ubangi province which borders the Central African Republic (CAR).

"We see pockets of Ebola generally going down, but unfortunately geographically it's spreading out," said World Health Organization Regional Director for Africa Mohamed Yakub Janabi in an interview with The Associated Press in Beni, eastern Congo, on Friday.
It's currently the deadliest outbreak in Congo's history with authorities recording at least 9,400 cases, including over 4,500 deaths, in the outbreak declared in mid-May.
The current epidemic is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a rare type of Ebola that has no approved vaccine or treatment.

Ebola is spread between people by direct contact with bodily fluids. It can cause fever, fatigue, and muscle pain, followed by vomiting and diarrhea. Some patients also develop internal or external bleeding.
Congo's Ebola crisis: Fear, mistrust and a growing outbreak

articles.title: Canada's Einarson wins 7th Grand Slam of Curling title, 1st since 2024
articles.summary: Kerri Einarson won her seventh Grand Slam of Curling title and first in two years, beating South Korea's Team Kang 6-3 in the women's final at the Co-op Invitational in Victoria on Sunday.

image.caption: Canadian skip Kerri Einarson, pictured at the world championships last March in Calgary. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Breaking
Kerri Einarson won her seventh Grand Slam of Curling title and first in two years, beating South Korea's Team Kang 6-3 in the women's final at the Co-op Invitational in Victoria on Sunday.
New-look rink never trailed en route to 1st Grand Slam title together
Einarson's new-look rink never trailed en route to its first Grand Slam title together. Her team from Gimli, Man., consists of third Shannon Birchard, second Karlee Burgess and lead Jocelyn Peterman.

Team Kang, skipped by Kim Kyeong-ae, tied the game at 2-2 in the third end after Einarson scored singles in the first two, but the five-time Tournament of Hearts champion responded by scoring two with her final shot in the fourth.
Einarson added another deuce in the sixth after holding Kim to a single in the fifth.
Kerri Einarson captures 7th Grand Slam title with victory over Team Kang at Co-op Invitational
Top-ranked Yannick Schwaller of Switzerland will face Norway’s Magnus Ramsfjell in the men’s final later Sunday.

The Co-op Invitational is the first of five stops on a newly compressed Grand Slam of Curling tour that will be completed before Christmas. The next stop is the Masters in Medicine Hat, Alta., from Nov. 3-8.
More to come.

articles.title: Liberals and Conservatives urge 'decisive' Alberta referendum vote to remain in Canada
articles.summary: With Alberta's referendum vote on Monday, federal Liberals and Conservatives are on the same page, each hoping to put to bed any question of the province's place in Canada.

image.caption: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, left, speaks about national unity in Calgary on Friday, the day after Prime Minister Mark Carney, right, attends a Forever Canadian rally in Calgary. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics
With Alberta's referendum vote on Monday, federal Liberals and Conservatives are on the same page, each hoping to put to bed any question of the province's place in Canada.
Ottawa wants to put separatism to bed, but polls show most Albertans have doubts
In the final days leading to the Alberta referendum, federal Liberals and Conservatives are on the same page, each hoping to put to bed any question of the province's place in Canada.
On Monday, Albertans will vote on whether they want to remain a province in Canada or start the legal process toward holding a binding referendum on leaving the country.
In their respective campaigning efforts, the government and the Official Opposition have urged Albertans to decisively vote to remain.

items: 'Vote like Canada depends on it,' Carney says at Calgary rally ahead of Alberta referendum

blocks.text: Prime Minister Mark Carney headlined a rally in Calgary on Thursday where he called for "a decisive result on Monday to settle this question."

Conservative MP Dane Lloyd — the caucus lead for the party's own Conservatives for Canada campaign — made an equivalent appeal in an exclusive interview on Rosemary Barton Live that aired Sunday morning.
"We need to ensure that every patriotic Canadian, Albertan gets out to vote so that we can have an overwhelmingly decisive vote for a stronger Alberta within a united Canada," Lloyd said.

Liberal MP Corey Hogan said there's likely no "magic number" that would put the issue of Alberta separation to rest. He told CBC's Rosemary Barton that the measure for success is whether there will be "an understanding from all political actors in this province that we can never do this again."
'Albertans are not quitters,' Poilievre tells Calgary conference

Recent polling from Abacus Data suggests that 68 per cent of voters would opt to keep Alberta a province of Canada, while 24 per cent would vote to start the legal process to hold a binding referendum on separating from the country.

The Abacus survey, which was conducted from Oct. 7 to 13, polled 1,021 Alberta voters. The survey's data was weighted according to census data, to ensure its sample matched Alberta's population. The margin of error for a comparable probability-based random sample of the same size is approximately plus or minus 3.1 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

Still, the polling suggests that most voters don't expect Monday's referendum will reliably bookend the issue. Abacus found that 61 per cent of the survey's respondents said at some point, they expect to vote again on Alberta separation after Monday.
According to Hogan, who represents the riding of Calgary Confederation, a separatist sentiment is just a reality in Alberta.
"Alberta separatism has been a thing my entire life," he said.

items: Danielle Smith has said no to a second referendum. But that decision might not be hers to make
Poilievre urges Albertans to embrace Canada: 'We don’t take our ball and go home'

blocks.text: "It's always been a reality worth addressing, it's always been a problem that there's a number of people in Alberta who have concerns with the country as a whole," Hogan said. "But it's not realistic to say this is going to go to zero, because it's never been at zero in Alberta."

Hogan added that "we need to make sure that there are political consequences to this," suggesting Albertans have become increasingly frustrated with their provincial government for carrying out the referendum process.

"We're going to have to see where this all is on Oct. 20," he said. "I'm certainly not calling the game at this particular moment, but it's very important that we as a province have a serious talk about how we ended up here in the first place."
For their part, Conservatives point to the Liberal government as a main irritant in Alberta's relationship with Canada.

Lloyd, who represents the Alberta riding of Parkland in Parliament, said he held roundtable discussions with Albertans as part of the Conservatives for Canada campaign, "and the message that I heard that was overwhelmingly clear was that people don't have a problem with Canada, they have a problem with Ottawa."
FULL SPEECH | Carney attends Forever Canadian rally in Calgary

At the same time, the current federal government hasn't been shy about acknowledging Ottawa's role in Albertan discontent. During his Thursday rally, Carney said that growing up in Alberta, "I remember how Ottawa made Albertans feel like our resources weren't our own."
"This is about Alberta feeling like its contributions haven't always been respected," Hogan said.
"We need to make sure that this whole country sees this whole country and that we are thinking about this whole country as we build policy for this country."
What about the other nine questions?
Listed before the consequential 10th question concerning a binding separation referendum, Monday's ballot notably includes nine others.

The first nine questions are focused on immigration and constitutional reform, including a query on whether Alberta should take more control over immigration, the responsibility for which is currently shared between the federal and provincial governments in Canada.
Quebec is alone in having distinct powers regarding the selection of its immigrants.

items: Who else besides Danielle Smith is saying 'yes to the nine' in Alberta's referendum?
Carney says Albertans should vote ‘No to the Nine’ in referendum

blocks.text: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has advocated for voters to choose "yes" on the ballot's first nine questions, while Carney was clear in urging Albertans to reject them.
Asked where the Conservatives stand on the first nine questions, Lloyd said the party's campaign has been "laser-focused" on the issue of a separation referendum "and that issue alone."

"Immigration has always involved federal-provincial conversations, and I think that they've been largely productive and largely fruitful," the Liberals' Hogan said. "We don't need people trying to hold guns to each other's heads to have constructive relationships in Canada."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
David Cummings is a reporter for CBC News.

articles.title: Inside Chicago's battle against the synthetic drugs flooding the US
articles.summary: A new wave of synthetic drugs is sweeping across the United States, raising fear of a worsening drug crisis. The BBC's Quentin Sommerville reports from the frontlines in South Side, Chicago, where…

blocks.text: Warning: This video contains descriptions of drug-taking and distressing images
A new wave of synthetic drugs is sweeping across the United States, raising fear of a worsening drug crisis.
Earlier this year, President Donald Trump pledged a crackdown on drug cartels, proscribing many as terrorist organisations.
Drug overdose deaths have fallen from a peak of around 110,000 in 2022, down to roughly 70,000 last year.

However, America's decades-long drug crisis may be accelerating and authorities are increasingly concerned about cheaper, more powerful synthetic drugs, including an animal tranquilliser called tranq.
The BBC's Quentin Sommerville reports from the frontlines in South Side, Chicago, where communities are battling the crisis.
Camera journalist: Darren Conway

articles.title: Cindy Crawford 'beyond heartbroken' after death of son Presley at 27
articles.summary: Presley Gerber's death in September is being investigated as a suspected overdose.

blocks.text: Supermodel Cindy Crawford has said she and her family are "beyond heartbroken" over the death of her son Presley Gerber.

"He is a sweet, beautiful soul who loved and is loved, now and forever," she posted on Instagram, next to a black-and-white photo of him. "We are so proud of how he showed up in the world, with kindness and vulnerability."
The 27-year-old died on 20 September at a rehab facility in California. Police said officials are investigating his death as a suspected overdose.
Gerber had been a model like his mother and younger sister Kaia, making his catwalk debut for Italian label Moschino aged just 16.
Crawford wrote in the post on Sunday: "We feel so blessed to have had Presley in our lives for 27 years."
"We are grateful for the outpouring of love and support from so many who know and love our family and even strangers who feel our pain," she also posted.
"Til we meet again our sweet boy. We love you forever, Mom, Dad and Kaia," she wrote in closing, with an emoji of angel wings.
The tribute also listed the dates of his birth and death.

The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner lists Gerber's case as pending additional investigation. The Santa Monica Police Department has said there is no indication foul play was involved in his death.

Gerber's sister Kaia also dedicated a post to him on Sunday which included a video of the two siblings as children dancing together, a photo of them standing near the ocean, and a four-page letter to "prez" typed out on a blue background.
In the letter, she said she had been scared of getting her ears pierced, so "you went first".
"But when I held the earring they took from your body, all I could think was: That belongs to you," she wrote.

"I am learning how to love you when I cannot see you," she also wrote. "How to tell you something without picking up my phone to call you. How to be your sister in a world that I can't reach for you in," she wrote.
In recent years, Gerber had spoken openly about his mental health challenges and drug use and frequently posted videos on Instagram himself for what he called "Mental Health Mondays".
His father Rande Gerber, a well-known businessman, co-founded the Casamigos tequila brand with George Clooney.
