articles.title: Parisians wake up to protest damage and looted shops
articles.summary: Violence broke out across France on Saturday during the latest day of demonstrations against conditions in schools and the cost of living.

blocks.text: Violence broke out across France on Saturday during the latest day of demonstrations against conditions in schools and the cost of living.
At least 1,200 people were arrested during what the French government described as an "escalation in violence", as shopfronts were smashed and stores looted.
For shop owners, this morning marks the start of clean-up efforts, with some reporting damages and stolen goods amount to €100,000 (£85,000).
The BBC's James Waterhouse reports from the streets of Paris outside damaged buildings.

articles.title: Is Germany's eight-hour workday under threat?
articles.summary: Would you work 12 hours straight? The CDU/CSU and SPD are locked in a dispute over reforms to the Working Hours Act. Workplace flexibility, collective bargaining agreements and worker protection…

image.caption: Leuna, in Saxony-Anhalt, has become one of Germany's major hubs for the chemical industry and oil refineriesImage: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS

blocks.text: The town of Leuna, in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, is one of the country's largest chemical industry hub, where more than 100 companies have established operations. Among them is the Finnish biotechnology group UPM, which has recently built a biorefinery for wood-based chemicals in Leuna. It's now hiring.

One of the job listings is for a chemical technician to oversee the rollout of new facilities. But to qualify, candidates must be willing to work 12-hour shifts. Is that legal? According to German law, standard working hours are limited to eight hours per day. It is permissible to extend this to ten hours, provided that workers receive compensatory time off for the overtime, and there must be at least 11 hours of rest between two shifts.
Twelve-hour shifts? What German law permits
Business associations and the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) parties have long called for these rules to be made more flexible.

Rainer Dulger, president of the Confederation of German Employers' Associations (BDA), points to the European Working Time Directive, which allows for a maximum weekly working time of 48 hours. "The allowance is being taken advantage of almost everywhere else — except here," Dulger told the dpa news agency in August.

Companies say they often find the existing rules too rigid, particularly in industries with seasonal fluctuations — such as tourism — or in project-based work, or during irregular peaks in workload, such as in the restaurant industry. They could deploy their staff more efficiently, says Dulger: "The Working Hours Act dates back to the era of fax machines and rotary-dial phones. It knows nothing of laptops or daycare hours."
4-day workweek: A model for the future?
CDU and SPD divided on working hours

In their 2025 coalition agreement, the CDU/CSU and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) agreed to reform the Working Hours Act. "In keeping with the European Working Time Directive, we want to allow for a maximum weekly rather than daily working time — also and especially to promote a better work-life balance," the agreement said.

The SPD would have preferred to leave the law unchanged, but had to accept the conservative parties' plans. The Social Democrats pointed out that longer working hours are already permitted in exceptional cases, such as in emergency services, the health care sector and security services. Workers in power plants, refineries and the chemical industry are also allowed to work up to 12 hours at a time.
A surprise for Chancellor Friedrich Merz

Even Chancellor Friedrich Merz himself seemed unaware of this exception until quite recently. After visiting the UPM refinery in Leuna in September, he recounted to business leaders at the German Employers' Day in Berlin that he was "completely surprised" to learn that the facilities operate on a continuous 12-hour shift schedule, thanks to the approval of the works council.

Merz recounted the shift supervisor describing the work schedule as "really great" — with three-day work weeks. "He said we have plenty of time for our families — it's a great way to organize things." Merz went on to conclude that this demonstrates the benefits of relaxing the Working Hours Act.

"Working more than eight hours is not exploitation. Rather, it can be a good opportunity to organize working hours more flexibly — both for businesses and for the people working there," the chancellor said. "We should do it."
SPD agrees to longer working hours, but with conditions

But there is resistance from within the SPD and from trade unions opposed to amending the Working Hours Act. The trade union Verdi argues that significantly longer workdays would have negative consequences for employees' health and would disadvantage people with family and caregiving responsibilities. In certain industries, employees could also be put under pressure to accept longer shifts.
An initial reform draft was drawn up in June 2026 by the Labor and Social Affairs Ministry, headed at the time by Bärbel Bas, an SPD politician who has since resigned for personal reasons.

The draft includes some conditions, including a collective bargaining agreement between employers and unions if any schedule changes were made, as well as health and safety regulations, and working hours to be tracked electronically.

blocks.caption: Bärbel Bas' reform plan had the CDU up in armsImage: Christophe Gateau/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Dispute over collective bargaining rights and worker protection

Annika Klose, spokesperson for labor and social policy for the SPD parliamentary group, explained the thinking behind the idea. Flexibility, she said, is "not a one-way street." The coalition agreement explicitly aims to promote a better balance between family and work. "So that it's sometimes possible to take your child to football practice in the afternoon and then continue working afterward — but not that my boss tells me against my will: 'You're working the shift from 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. tomorrow.'"

The CDU/CSU immediately rejected the draft. Businesses were also up in arms. "This draft must be withdrawn and completely revised," demanded Dulger in a statement, saying it was "steeped in mistrust." The German Confederation of Skilled Crafts (ZDH) spoke of a "breach of the commitments agreed to in the coalition agreement." The reform has been on hold ever since.
Why the reform stalled
At the Employers' Day event, Merz held out the prospect of progress. "This is indeed long overdue. I believe we can accomplish this relatively quickly and create flexibility in the labor market."

It remains to be seen, however, whether the new SPD Labor Minister, Alexander Schweitzer, shares this view. In early October, his party released a paper on reforming working hours that read like a declaration of war against the CDU. "Self-determination, Not Deregulation" is the title of the seven-page document that was signed by the SPD working group on labor, the youth organization Jusos, the "60plus" working group and the women's wing of the SPD.

In the paper, the Social Democrats not only reiterate the points that already appeared in Bas' draft back in June. They also demand that, in the future, employers and employees should decide on working hours "jointly and by mutual agreement." They argued that it is not "in the spirit of a modern reform of working time law" if only employers can determine when employees finish work.

From a political perspective, the dispute over reforming work hours has long become more than just a debate over legal provisions. It is a fundamental dispute over how much flexibility workers should be expected to tolerate in the future and to what extent the state should protect them. And it is yet another stumbling block for the already beleaguered government in Berlin.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Hilarious quips and ‘100,000-volt’ energy: the hypemen (and women) redefining Afrobeats music
articles.summary:
Style of emceeing based on high-octane, ad-libbed vocals has flourished thanks to its unique way of captivating crowds

For the 2015 freshmen cohort of the history degree programme at the…

blocks.text: For the 2015 freshmen cohort of the history degree programme at the University of Lagos, their classmate’s first-semester presentation was so captivating that they began calling him Toby Shang, after the 16th-century Chinese dynasty he had focused on.

His crowd engagement that day had been harnessed from his high school days as a ginger-man (energiser) in a three-man band and as a private tutor. By his final year at university, his viral catchphrases and infectious energy had resulted in a hit song, Shedibalabala. Today, he is one of the self-acclaimed “evangelists and pioneers” in the Afrobeats sub-genre some are now calling Afrohype or lamba.

blocks.caption: Toby Shang by the waterfront in the Lagos suburb of Akoka. Photograph: Sogo Oladele/The Guardian

blocks.text: “Even my mother calls me Shang now,” the 32-year-old, born Tobi Michael Adeyeye, said in an interview near the university’s lagoon waterfront, where he once emceed gatherings.
Since then he has hosted his own rave, released two EPs and run four editions of his School of Hype – a one-day masterclass with online mentoring that has launched several rising stars.
Allow TikTok content?

This article includes content provided by TikTok. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Hypemen neither sing nor rap entirely, but perform high-octane ad-libbed vocals “and onomatopoeic sounds” over fresh beats or popular instrumentals such as Dorime, a made-in-Nigeria version of 1996’s Ameno by the French group Era, a song that has become a continental nightclub classic. In response, nightclub patrons donate or spray money – the Nigerian custom of throwing or placing money on someone to celebrate them.

Hype is now omnipresent at wedding after-parties, raves and corporate parties. On Instagram, one teenage sensation is now known for recording 30-second hypes for birthday celebrants at the request of friends or relatives.

blocks.caption: Toby Shang made a name for himself while still a student at the University of Lagos. Photograph: Sogo Oladele/The Guardian

blocks.text: “Hypemen have the gift of the gab and fine mic control,” said the London-based doctor and cultural critic Dami Ajayi, who encountered one at a party in Tirana last month. “He used the spaces between lyrics for hilarious quips, many of which were frontally risque and misogynistic,” he said.

Despite being a male-dominated sub-genre, a few women have made their mark, such as the Yaoundé-based bikutsi artist Lady Ponce, known as the “100,000-volt lady” because of her energy. Other notable female figures in the scene include Deborah ‘Hype Queen Baddy’ Francis – an alumnus of Shang’s school who died in September – and the radio presenter Melody “M.I.A” Adigo, both from Lagos.

The art of hyping as it is known in west and central Africa has its roots in praise-singing and call-and-response music styles ingrained for centuries in Black populations on both sides of the Atlantic. In west Africa, this tradition took the form of oral historians known as griots. In the US, it was sustained by negro spirituals, sacred folk songs created by enslaved African Americans.
after newsletter promotion
These styles laid the foundation for the atalaku (meaning “look here, look at me” in the Kikongo language of the DR Congo) tradition that came alive in 1980s Kinshasa, followed by today’s hype scene.
Exponents of this style include the American gospel singer Kirk Franklin as well as the Congolese rumba bandleader Koffi Olomide and the Congolese singer Awilo Longomba.

The success of Olomide and Longomba at the turn of the 21st century set off a craze in Côte d’Ivoire, where coupé-décalé music embraced the atalaku trend alongside farotement, the act of showing off by throwing cash at performers or guests at parties.

blocks.caption: The Congolese singer Koffi Olomide performing at a festival in Abidjan in September 2021.  Photograph: Sia Kambou/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: A line encouraging audiences to gallop like a horse in the Ivorian star DJ Arafat’s 2003 viral homage to a late friend – “Tout le monde galope, kirikata kirikata” – influenced later hits from Nigerian Afrobeats musicians Flavour N’abania and Skales.

Côte d’Ivoire’s national television network, RTI, ran an atalaku talent hunt for several years. Lili Djely, an Ivorian woman of Malian origin, won the 2006 edition with a mix of Ivorian nouchi and French, defeating men to take the crown. In recent years, an MC/hypeman of the year category was introduced at the Ghana DJ awards as hype flourished there too.

Thanks to the success of Afrobeats, Afrohype is now widely recognised as a full-time career. As artists became more expensive to book after Covid-19, promoters turned to hypemen – previously criticised for simply doing voiceovers. Some are now reportedly paid as much as 5-8m naira (£2,844–4,550) for a 30-minute or one-hour performance.
Some observers, however, say hype is a nuisance, amping up noise levels at events or encouraging fraudulent lifestyles, and that many performers do not customise language and tempo to fit the event.

blocks.caption: The Congolese musician Awilo Longomba performing at the All Africa music awards in Lagos in November 2019.  Photograph: Pius Utomi Ekpei/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: Nevertheless, hypemen are now a permanent fixture on the entertainment scene. For Shang, they are helping fun-seekers and club-goers get back on the dancefloor.

“People are facing a lot of challenges … they need somebody to tell them money is coming in the new week,” he said. “Also, everybody wants to press their phones or show Birkin bags in clubs. Nobody wants to dance because dancing is seen as for small kids. You need a hypeman to bring out that childlike part in every person. A 60-year-old woman can start dancing like a young girl if the hype is good enough.”

articles.title: Sudbury artist who created temporary Jesus head sculpture 10 years ago has risen above the furor
articles.summary: In October 2016, Sudbury, Ont., artist Heather Wise generated headlines worldwide with her temporary restoration of a local Jesus statue. A decade on, Wise is finally able to laugh about it.

image.caption: Sudbury artist Heather Wise holds up the keychains based on her temporary Jesus head sculpture that captured headlines around the world 10 years ago. (Kate Rutherford/CBC)

blocks.text: Sudbury
In October 2016, Sudbury, Ont., artist Heather Wise generated headlines worldwide with her temporary restoration of a local Jesus statue. A decade on, Wise is finally able to laugh about it.
A decade after her art restoration went viral for the wrong reasons, Heather Wise has embraced her notoriety
Sudbury artist Heather Wise twirls a key chain with a tiny, terracotta-coloured head dangling on the end. It’s a small memento of what has come to be known as the Temporary Jesus Head incident.
A decade ago, Wise first created that unusual head in clay to fix a vandalized statue at a local church.

It did not go according to plan. The resulting furor put Sudbury, Ont., on the international map for a time, and attracted all kinds of attention for Wise. It's only now, 10 years after her creation caused headlines around the world, that Wise is finally ready for an interview.
“I became one of the most infamous, famous artists on the planet,” she said recently.

Wise's involvement in the story started in October 2016, when she crafted a replacement for a missing marble head of a statue of baby Jesus cradled in Mary's arms on the front lawn of Sainte-Anne-des-Pins Catholic Church in downtown Sudbury.
A year earlier someone had made off with the son of God's head, and Wise said seeing the decapitated baby had made her sad.
“I was just going to make a temporary head to give it dignity, and spend all winter learning how to carve a stone head,” she said.
Artist Heather Wise says this temporary clay head was never meant to be the final fix for the statue, but it attracted attention right away. (Marina von Stackelberg/CBC)
It also occurred to her that it would be a way to show her talent.

"In my head I was thinking, 'Wow, an opportunity to do a gig for a depiction of Christ for the Catholic Church'," she said. "This is a good part of my resume. I had no idea it would become internationally famous."
With the blessing of the parish priest, she mocked up a head using dollar store clay, a notably darker medium than the white marble of the statue.
The head featured a large nose, thick neck and spiky crown.
“All in all, I don’t think he’s ugly,” Wise said in a recent interview. “I think he’s got a unique look.”
The priest at the time, Father Gérard Lajeunnesse, told reporters he appreciated Wise’s offer.

“The pose is a bit unnatural, and, I think, around the mouth, the upper lip is maybe a bit in too much, but of course it's a first try and hopefully whatever is done at the end will please everyone,” he said.
But the new head quickly attracted unfavourable comparisons to a Simpsons character or a chia pet.
Almost overnight, a Facebook post went viral with 14 million views, prompting mockery in the comments and triggering international media coverage.
Father Lajeunesse went on to do interviews with CBC Radio's As it Happens, The Toronto Star, CNN, The Guardian and The Daily Mail.
Wise did not offer interviews — until now.
“A lot of the media was not exactly nice,” she said. “One headline was, ‘Someone commissioned the worst artist in the world’ when you didn't see any of my other art. So how would you know?”
Memes adapting Wise's temporary Jesus head quickly spread. (TemporaryJesusHead/Instagram)
Wise's creation did not last long. When the clay started to dissolve in the rain, staining the marble, it was returned to Wise, who still has it.
The statue's original marble head was eventually returned to the church and re-attached. The furor died down.
In the years since, Wise has come to terms with becoming the butt of so many jokes.

"Some of the bullying was just straight up mean," Wise said. "But these are people that you don't know, know nothing about you. And also when you don't take things personally, you can distance that negative energy from you. And we have that power in our mind."
Now she can laugh at the memes, one of which placed the clay head on then-prime minister Justin Trudeau, another on Darth Vader.
The local art community rallied around her, Wise said, with some even getting tattoos of the head.
A student made a three-dimensional temporary Jesus head mask for a theatre project for university.

items: Temporary statue head of baby Jesus back in hands of Sudbury artist
Statue's temporary Jesus head garners international attention

blocks.text: Then a Sudbury garage band called Strange Attractor wrote a song thanking her for making the head.
“These guys have toured Europe and when I heard it, I loved that song,” she said.
What pleases her most, perhaps, is being mentioned in art magazine articles. There was one about botched restorations.

“For instance, somebody grabbed Tutankhamun's death mask beard, broke it off and tried to fix it with crazy glue,” she said. “Somebody painted the Lord Buddha statues like they're out of a candy shop.”
Sudbury artist Heather Wise shows off some of her original artwork in her studio. (Kate Rutherford/CBC)
Another article featuring her head, she said, was about art that was so bad, it was good.
Temporary Jesus Head even appeared in a German book about art accidents, she said.

“They said with all the cyber bullying, Heather Wise did what Jesus would have done: I responded with love,” she said of the book. “Well, I'm not Jesus. Whoa, that's blasphemous. But wow, what a complimentary comparison.”
A final upshot of the Temporary Jesus Head incident is that the previously agnostic Wise has begun going to church — and is even thinking about becoming a Catholic.
“What I love about Christianity, is that we're all imperfect," she said. "I feel so free not judging people.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Kate Rutherford is a reporter with CBC News in Sudbury, covering northern Ontario. News tips can be sent to kate.rutherford@cbc.ca

articles.title: How reliant is Ukraine on the US-controlled Starlink internet service?
articles.summary: Kyiv keeps issuing warnings that the satellite internet system Starlink is being restricted in Ukraine. How dependent is the country on the system, and what would happen if it went down?

image.caption: The Starlink satellite internet system has become a core component of Ukrainian defenseImage: Adam88/Pond5 Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: Few technological systems have played such an important role in the war in Ukraine as Starlink, central to the communications, reconnaissance and drone operations of the Ukrainian armed forces. There are currently widespread concerns that Elon Musk's satellite internet service in Ukraine may be restricted or even switched off. In recent days, Kyiv has repeatedly reported disruptions and restrictions affecting its use.
How Starlink enables communications

Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, Ukraine has made extensive use of the satellite internet service, which is operated by the US company SpaceX. With it, military personell can continue to communicate and exchange data, even when infrastructure has been destroyed or cellphone networks are down.

According to the Center for Security Studies (CSS) at ETH Zurich, around 50,000 Starlink terminals were in use in Ukraine in 2025. These are the system's specialised receiving and transmitting devices, which enable communications on the battlefield. They are also used to relay orders between command levels and receive drone footage.

The importance of the Starlink network can in part be explained by events at the beginning of the war. According to a CSS analysis, the KA-SAT satellite system previously favored by Ukraine was targeted in a cyberattack just hours before Russia's invasion. Starlink quickly became a vital alternative.
Starlink and Starshield: civilian versus military use
When discussing current affairs, the terms "Starlink" and "Starshield" are often used interchangeably.

blocks.caption: There are around 50,000 Starlink terminals in UkraineImage: Christoph Soeder/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: However, Starlink is SpaceX's commercial satellite internet service, whereas Starshield is specifically designed for governmental and military use. While based on the same technological infrastructure, it is designed for security and defense applications.

This distinction matters, because the latest reports of restrictions seem to primarily concern systems used for military purposes. Elon Musk recently stated that Starshield systems are controlled by the US government, whereas Starlink is a commercial service operated by SpaceX.
The role of Starlink in drone warfare
Alongside communications, Starlink is mainly used for drone operations. The system provides an internet connection for ground, naval and aerial drones.

This connection means video footage can be transmitted almost in real time, while drones can be controlled over long distances. Ukraine uses these systems for reconnaissance and attacks deep behind enemy lines.
According to ETH Zurich, images and GPS coordinates of Russian positions are also transmitted via these communication channels. The data is sent to artillery units and used to coordinate operations.
What throttling Starlink would mean

According to Ukrainian media reports, on Tuesday night, SpaceX temporarily introduced a speed restriction for Starlink terminals in Ukraine, limiting terminals in motion to a speed of about 160 kilometers per hour (100 mph).

Such a restriction has direct consequences for fast-moving Ukrainian drones, some of which travel at speeds of up to 300 kilometers per hour (186 mph). If the connection to the drone is lost, live video footage can no longer be transmitted, and the systems can no longer be controlled in real time. The drones effectively have to continue their mission while flying blind.
Did someone order Ukraine's high-speed Starlink shutdown?
Restricting or even shutting down a Starlink network would therefore not only make communication more difficult. It would also affect Ukrainian drone operations, and other military activities.
More than just satellite internet

However, Starlink and its military counterpart, Starshield, are only one essential component of Ukraine's defense system. Ukraine also receives reconnaissance data from western partners, including information about Russian air attacks, missile launches, troop movements and anti-aircraft positions, as well as potential routes to avoid them.

This information helps with air defense and offensive operations. Without this intelligence, it would be significantly harder for Ukraine to carry out long-range drone operations against targets in Russian territory.

The two elements are particularly effective when combined. Reconnaissance data provides information about potential targets and routes, while Starlink ensures that this data can be quickly relayed to units.

This is why reports that the US is limiting access to its reconnaissance data are as worrying as the possibility that Starlink might be throttled. Other NATO countries, such as the United Kingdom and France, can also provide reconnaissance data, but not to the extent as the United States.
Strategic dependence
Europe has several alternatives to Starlink, including Eutelsat/OneWeb. However, their ability to match Starlink's performance in wartime conditions has not yet been tested on a large scale.

blocks.caption: Starlink terminals enable mobile internet connection on the battlefield for the operation of dronesImage: Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP

blocks.text: The recurrent concern about possible restrictions makes clear that satellite communications have become a central component of Ukrainian defense. And while relying on a single provider simplifies operations, it also shows how dependent modern armed forces have become on private technology companies. Experts say this marks a fundamental change in warfare.
Meanwhile, Ukraine's successful use of Starlink has helped the system to achieve global recognition.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: Freeland believes her resignation led to better outcome for Trudeau, allowing him to exit before likely defeat
articles.summary: Former finance minister and deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland believes her resignation — which spurred Justin Trudeau to step down — was ultimately a good outcome for the former prime minister…

image.caption: Former deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland gets a shout-out from then-prime minister Justin Trudeau during a caucus meeting on Parliament Hill in Ottawa in April 2024. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Former finance minister and deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland believes her resignation — which spurred Justin Trudeau to step down — was ultimately a good outcome for the former prime minister given his plummeting popularity.
In CBC interview, former finance minister defends her record and says history will look kindly on Trudeau

While her book, Unreliable Boyfriend, is meant to be a guide for dealing with U.S. President Donald Trump's administration, it also outlines how her political relationship with Trudeau declined in the final months of his government.

Freeland writes that the prime minister informed her in a Zoom call that he would be replacing her as finance minister just days before she was set to deliver the government's fall economic statement in late 2024.
She abruptly stepped down the same day the statement was to be tabled in Parliament. Trudeau resigned a few weeks later.

items: In Unreliable Boyfriend, Chrystia Freeland details the rift between her and Trudeau

blocks.text: Her book outlines how a conversation with former Liberal prime minister Jean Chrétien a month earlier helped her make the ultimate decision to leave.
Speaking to CBC's The Sunday Magazine, Freeland detailed another conversation she had with Chrétien in the wake of the blow-up.

"Prime minister Chrétien said … in resigning, it was ultimately a better outcome for Canada, for the Liberal Party — and also ultimately for prime minister Trudeau because it allowed him not to lead our party to defeat," Freeland told host Piya Chattopadhyay.
"I think that is a very wise observation."

The Conservatives held a huge lead in the polls over Trudeau's Liberals during the final year of his tenure. Mark Carney won the Liberal leadership race to replace Trudeau and led the party to another election win in 2025.

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance Chrystia Freeland rises to present the federal budget in the House of Commons in Ottawa as Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, lower right, listens on April 16, 2024. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)
Freeland defends record as finance minister
Freeland had been a cabinet minister in Trudeau's government since it was first elected in 2015 and served as finance minister from the summer of 2020 until her resignation.

When asked if she felt she bore any responsibility for the fading popularity of the Trudeau government — given that the Conservative surge was driven by their focus on the economy and cost of living — she touted her record as finance minister.
LISTEN | Chrystia Freeland on The Sunday Magazine:
The Sunday Magazine43:02Chrystia Freeland talks Trump, Canada-U.S. trade war and political tenure with Trudeau
"I am very glad that as finance minister, I got us through COVID and I preserved our AAA credit rating while doing that," she said.
"We were able to return to a sustainable fiscal path. Now, that was politically hard to do, but it was absolutely the right thing to do."

Despite their political fallout, Freeland spoke kindly of her early political relationship with Trudeau. And, as she notes in her book, she argued that history will look kindly on Trudeau — but added that she wished he had stepped down earlier.
Justin Trudeau and Chrystia Freeland over the years

She insisted multiple times in the interview that Unreliable Boyfriend is "not a book about Justin Trudeau." But she didn't directly answer if she had reached out to her former boss during the writing process.

"I chose what I wrote really carefully. It was important for me to be authentic and to be open. But this really is a book about me and a book about my ideas and my view of where we should go," she said.
"It's not a salacious story."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Major is a senior writer for CBC's parliamentary bureau in Ottawa. He previously worked as a digital reporter for CBC Ottawa and a producer for CBC's Power & Politics. He holds a master's degree in journalism and a bachelor's degree in public affairs and policy management, both from Carleton University. He also holds a master's degree in arts from Queen's University. He can be reached at darren.major@cbc.ca.
Interview produced by Sarah-Joyce Battersby

articles.title: Doing the dishes and riding the subway? Why the royals keep trying to look relatable
articles.summary: Members of the Royal Family are offering glimpses into their everyday lives, the most recent examples of attempts to deal with a fundamental challenge that is a priority for the monarchy: how to…

image.caption: Catherine, Princess of Wales, left, laughs as she talks with Lynda Jones, right, who offered her a potato chip at a weekly lunch club in Pulborough, southern England, on Sept. 30. During that visit, Catherine mentioned to seniors that she and Prince William do the dishes together at home. (Arthur Ed

blocks.text: It all seemed a bit prosaic, really, chatting about doing the dishes with her husband or riding on the subway with her daughter.

But there was Catherine, Princess of Wales, telling seniors how she and Prince William share the washing-up duties, and a few days later, taking a trip on the London Underground with Princess Charlotte.

Beyond that glimpse into their everyday lives, though, these recent moments reflect an attempt to deal with a longstanding and more fundamental challenge that is a priority for the monarchy: how to appear relatable to a public that lives far beyond royal walls.
"The monarchy isn't trying to convince us that William and Catherine are ordinary people," royal historian Justin Vovk said in an interview.
"It's about trying to convince us that despite extraordinary circumstances, they experience the same human concerns as everybody else."
Efforts to do that convincing have long been a priority for monarchies throughout Europe.

Catherine, Princess of Wales, right, sits with residents onboard a West Sussex Minibus, a volunteer-led community transport group, during a visit to Pulborough, southern England, on Sept. 30. (Arthur Edwards/AFP/Getty Images)

"Since … the political upheavals of the 19th century, which saw various monarchs … losing their thrones … there was a real consciousness that you no longer needed just the support of the elite, you needed to be relatable," said Judith Rowbotham, a social and cultural scholar and visiting research professor at the University of Plymouth in southwestern England, in an interview.
"Queen Victoria writes her highland journal — suitably sanitized — but that's an attempt to make herself relatable."

What's thought of as relatable nearly 200 years ago differs from what William and Catherine and other working royals may try to do or show today. But the overall significance is the same, Rowbotham suggests.
"Relatability is something that modern monarchies, certainly modern European monarchies, see as genuinely important," she said.

"Particularly at a time when people are worried about money, when people are questioning government actions over taxes … the fact that yes, they live in a lavish house, but they live ordinary lives in a lavish house … that's the impression they want to give, that they don't have live-in staff, they're not surrounded by flunkies and footmen."
As much as there is that desire to appear relatable, there is little to suggest it can ultimately eliminate the actual separation between the monarchy and the public.

This 1969 photo is one of a series taken to show the informal life of Prince Charles, centre, as he sits with Queen Elizabeth, background centre, Prince Philip, second from left, Prince Edward, left, Princess Anne, background, and then Prince Andrew, right, at Sandringham House, in Sandringham, England. (The Associated Press)
"There will always be distance between the monarchy and the people," said Vovk.
"But all of [it], stretching from Queen Victoria up to William and Catherine is about trying to close as much of the distance as they can that is within their control."
And there's a basic reason behind that, Vovk suggests.
"The monarchy's relevance, its viability, is now predicated on its perceived relatability and accessibility," he said.

"People don't want a Royal Family that is distant and isolated and feels unfamiliar. They want a Royal Family that they feel they can connect with, that they feel like if they were to bump into them on the street, they could just go up to them and talk to them."
That, however, creates something of a paradox.

"If you strip away all of the pomp and the pageantry and some of the mystique around royalty, it raises the question of what makes it so special, anyway? Why have it at all?" Vovk said. "So it is a balancing act."

Pomp and pageantry are on full display as King Charles, left, and Queen Camilla, right, make their way along the Mall following their coronation on May 6, 2023, in London, England. (Charles McQuillan/The Associated Press)
Other factors can play into the monarchy's focus on relatability at any given time.

Queen Victoria's seclusion, particularly after the death of her husband, Prince Albert, drove concerns about relatability during her reign. Rowbotham sees another circumstance closely connected to the monarch at play right now.
"We don't know how long Charles is going to be around, given that he's in his 70s, given that he is still being treated for cancer," she said.
"This time, it's a question of assuring the monarchy's survival by making it clear that there is an heir who is well-prepared and ready to take over the duty.
"That's why I think … they're paying so much attention to the whole issue" of relatability, Rowbotham said.

items: With move to 'forever home,' Prince and Princess of Wales could offer hint of 'more egalitarian' monarchy

blocks.text: Vovk sees a greater level of transparency from the current royals compared to previous generations when it comes to relatability.

"We're seeing the curtain being pulled back on the aspects of royal life that are no different or at least have minimal difference from the average person — so, you know, siblings bickering, not liking doing chores, spouses sharing domestic responsibilities."
On the constitutional or political side of the monarchy, however, he sees less revelation.

"There's still some degree of gatekeeping going on here with what amount of royal life is being disclosed and what isn't. That will always be the case with something that is connected with the political life of the nation."
Passing a robot controller to a prince

Benjamin Santiago, left, teaches Prince Edward, right, how to drive a robot using a controller at Queen's Park in Toronto on Oct. 2. (Grant and Martin Curtis/Duke of Edinburgh's International Award — Canada)
Benjamin Santiago had never had an experience like it.

"It's not every day that you get to give a robot controller to royalty and teach them how to drive it," the Grade 12 student at St. Joseph's Catholic High School in London, Ont., said in an interview.
Benjamin, a 17-year-old member of the school robotics team, had that opportunity earlier this month when he passed the controller to Prince Edward, the Duke of Edinburgh, at an event in Toronto.

The gathering that drew education leaders, school board representatives, industry partners and students to Queen's Park highlighted the recent announcement by the provincial Ministry of Education to expand access to the Duke of Edinburgh Award program to schools across Ontario. That comes as the award, founded by Edward's late father, Prince Philip, is evolving and working to blend trades and skills-based experiences into public education to boost opportunities for young Canadians.

"It was amazing. I'm super grateful," Benjamin said of his opportunity to meet Edward. "The prince was super enthusiastic and really just interested about who we are and what our goals were as Ontario students."
In the royal encounter, Benjamin saw the potential to boost support for an area of education close to his heart.

Benjamin says Prince Edward was 'super enthusiastic and really just interested about who we are and what our goals were as Ontario students.' (Grant and Martin Curtis/Duke of Edinburgh's International Award — Canada)

"If someone like the prince can feel the controller and feel how it is to be an engineer in high school and then later on become an engineer in post-secondary … the funding towards programs like robotics may increase."
Edward has had a longstanding interest in youth and promoting opportunities for them, something that has been a frequent focus on his visits to Canada.

"He really took the time to really focus his attention on the students, which is something that I really personally admired about this, but also to make sure that every student felt seen and heard," Laura Briscoe, senior director for business development, communications and experiential education for the Duke of Edinburgh's International Award — Canada, said in an interview.

"He wants to know the realities of youth in Canada and how the award can support their lifelong learning and development, and I found him to be very responsive and open to hearing feedback, whether it's constructive feedback, what are the barriers, where are the gaps, what are we missing?"

items: More 'soft power signals': On heels of King's visit, Prince Edward takes week-long trip to P.E.I., Ontario
Prince Edward makes royal visit to Canada — pandemic-style

blocks.text: The Queen's Park gathering was a "wonderful experience" for everyone there, said Kathy Cepo, Benjamin's chemistry teacher and one of his robotics coaches.
"The prince was so engaged with these students and they felt like they were the only people in the room," she said in an interview.
"He was praising them the entire time and so proud of them."
They meet again
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, left, speaks with King Charles, right, during an audience at Buckingham Palace in London on Wednesday. (Aaron Chown/Getty Images)
Few world leaders have shaken hands with King Charles as often as the president of Ukraine.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy was back in the U.K. this week, meeting Charles at Buckingham Palace on Wednesday.
"I thank His Majesty King Charles III for the audience," Zelenskyy posted afterward on X.
"It is important for me to have the opportunity to personally thank him for his unwavering support for Ukraine. We appreciate all the assistance provided by the United Kingdom."

It was his third meeting with the King this year, and came as the U.K. doubled down on support for Ukraine and called for its international partners to increase pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin to respect the U.S. call for an energy ceasefire.
The King meeting with Zelenskyy "on a bit of a consistent basis is a way of … reaffirming Britain's overall support for Ukraine, even though governments are changing," said Vovk.
"It's a way to reassure President Zelenskyy that the United Kingdom stands with Ukraine."
While a monarch is meant to be above politics, meeting with Zelenskyy would also come at the request of the U.K. government.
"The King isn't being party political, taking sides. He's doing his constitutional duty," said Rowbotham.
Prince Harry and Meghan step out in Nottingham

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, left, and Prince Harry, right, greet well-wishers as they arrive at the Community Recording Studio, a youth and community charity that offers a wide range of creative activities, sports, mentoring and youth development programs, in Nottingham, England, on Thursday. (Christopher Furlong/Getty Images)
They aren't official working members of the Royal Family anymore.

But the casual passerby could be forgiven for being a bit confused Thursday as Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, carried out events connected with their private charitable interests in the city where they did their first public outing as an engaged couple nearly a decade ago. It was their first joint appearance in public since they returned to the U.K. from California in late August.
"It's great to be back," Harry said. "Wonderful and great to be back ⁠in Nottingham, too."

items: Charles confirms Harry and Meghan to remain non-working royals after their return to U.K.

blocks.text: They began by visiting a recording studio run by a youth and community charity that has received support from a 1.1-​million-pound ($2.1-million Cdn) donation announced by Harry last year.

At their next stop at the Himmah charity, which tackles food poverty, Meghan was reunited with ​four contributors to a charity cookbook released to raise funds in the wake of London's 2017 Grenfell Tower fire disaster. She had donated 10,000 pounds ($18,800 Cdn) from the book's proceeds to help the Himmah hub.
Thursday's visit was the first pre-arranged and advertised occasion since their return, Rowbotham said, but it was not an official royal event.
Harry and Meghan moving back to the U.K.

"However, it was carefully arranged to ensure media reportage and a suitable turnout of sympathetic public by choosing a location — Nottingham — which was … where they were for their first post engagement royal visit."
But it was on a much different scale, she said.
"No local dignitaries were there in official capacity."
Vovk saw the visit as their first outing as part of "the new Sussex court."

He also sees the potential of a "problem of optics" for the monarchy where "Harry and Meghan are engaging in activities that to the average observer look really more or less the same [as] what the monarchy does."
Prince Harry and Meghan, Duke and Duchess of Sussex, visit the Himmah Hub in Nottingham, England, on Thursday. (Annabel Lee-Ellis/The Associated Press)
Vovk expects to see an escalation in public appearances and informal events from the senior working royals.

"I think the monarchy is now going to have to pick up the pace in terms of the kinds of engagements and public accessibility they're doing just in order to keep that clear distinction between Harry and Meghan [having] titles but they are technically private individuals from a legal, constitutional perspective," he said.

items: Why Prince Harry and Meghan face more challenges after their return to the U.K.
The 'shockwaves' of Prince Harry and Meghan's return to the U.K.

blocks.text: The biggest danger and concern for the royals, he said, is "that the brand itself could be misappropriated, misrepresented, in a way that has never really been a factor before."
Rowbotham doesn't see a threat to the institution itself, although she expects it will be discussed as such.
Royally quotable
"We like sitting quietly and reading. Occasionally, when I'm deep in a book, I'll hear him roaring with laughter about something."
— Queen Camilla, in a television documentary, offering some insight into the reading habits of her and her husband, King Charles.
Royal reads

Catherine, Princess of Wales, third from left, and Prince William, third from right, help behind the till during a visit to an Ikea store in Belfast, Northern Ireland, on Oct. 9. (Phil Noble/Getty Images)

British police say search ‌warrants they secured to search properties linked to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor had been issued unlawfully and must be quashed, but said the investigation into King Charles's younger brother was ongoing. [CBC]

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor faced a 1.8-million-pound ($3.4-million Cdn) bill to cover repair and restoration of his former Royal Lodge home in Windsor after the lease was officially surrendered. King Charles reportedly covered some of the costs. [The Guardian]
King Charles spoke of his "special connection" to Wales while delivering an address to the Welsh Parliament. [The Independent]

Zara Tindall has opened up about the tough-love upbringing she received from Princess Anne and Mark Phillips — including being told she would get no help when she decided to follow her parents into top-level equestrian sport. [Daily Mail]
The Prince and Princess of Wales met hundreds of royal fans in south Belfast as part of a surprise visit to Northern Ireland. [Belfast Telegraph]
Prince William brought traffic to a halt just down the road from Buckingham Palace to play cricket with some of the game's biggest names. [The Independent]
Prince William joins cricket stars for an informal game on The Mall in London, England, on Tuesday, in the leadup to the annual Earthshot Prize awards in Mumbai next month. (Isabel Infantes/Reuters)

articles.title: They don't make instant coffee like they used to. It's getting gourmet now
articles.summary: In a world of fancy espresso machines, gourmet blends and cold brews, instant coffee has often been considered at the bottom of the proverbial coffee barrel. But the powder is getting a glow-up,…

image.caption: Just Us! in Halifax has been selling premium instant coffee for over 15 years. But over the past couple years, it's seen a big boost in sales. (Harrison Newman Jardine)

blocks.text: Cost of Living

In a world of fancy espresso machines, gourmet blends and cold brews, instant coffee has often been considered at the bottom of the proverbial coffee barrel. But the powder is getting a glow-up, thanks to better quality, some social media trends, and advancements in instant coffee technology.
Instant coffee sales have increased across Canada in recent years
LISTEN | Why more people are drinking instant coffee:
Cost of Living5:23Instant coffee is having a moment

In a world of fancy espresso machines, gourmet blends and cold brews, instant coffee has often been considered to be at the bottom of the proverbial coffee barrel. But the powder is getting a glow-up, thanks to better quality, social media trends and advancements in instant coffee technology.
"It's having a moment," said Joey Pittoello, general manager of the coffee roaster Just Us! in Halifax. "I think people have discovered that instant coffee can be of much better quality now."
More brewers are choosing to highlight instant coffee, from big brands such as Starbucks, to smaller roasters like Just Us!, in part because they are seeing an increased demand for it.

At Just Us!, which has been selling instant coffee for over 15 years, instant coffee sales have grown around 15 per cent in the last two years, says Pittoello, with other coffee companies such as Eight Ounce Coffee and Canadian Heritage Coffee Roasters in Calgary reporting similar increases in recent years.
According to a 2025 Agricultural Canada report, instant coffee sales totalled $330 million in Canada in 2024, up 10 per cent from the previous year.
"Instant coffee is undergoing the same transformation as a lot of coffee drinks," said Robert Carter, a food industry analyst and the president of the Coffee Association of Canada.
"There's more premiumization that's taking place. And I think that's resulting in an increase in consumption."

Social media trends are also improving instant coffee's rep. There's the Dalgona coffee trend, popularized during the pandemic, which is a whipped drink made by whisking instant coffee, sugar and hot water, then putting it over milk.
People are also using instant coffee to make lattes or iced coffees at home. Additionally, Pittoello says people use it in baking, or in seasoning when barbecuing.
"It's easy to make interesting sweet milky drinks with instant coffee. You just have to add it, right?" said Pittoello.
A change in quality and technology
Instant coffee isn't anything new though. Big brands like Nescafé and Maxwell House have been selling instant coffee for decades.
"I don't think it ever really went anywhere," said Pittoello.
What has changed, though, is the quality of instant coffee. Pittoello says the robusta bean, which has a simple flavour profile compared to arabica, had commonly been used to make instant coffee.
"You're enhancing the level of low quality by turning it into instant coffee and that's really what defined instant coffee for decades," said Pittoello.
Joey Pittoello is the general manager of the coffee roaster Just Us! in Halifax. (Harrison Newman Jardine)
Now more specialty roasters are using better beans to make their instant coffee. Just Us! uses arabica, as does Starbucks.

But that's not the only reason you're seeing specialty coffee shops selling their own instant coffee. Josh Hockin, head of coffee at Eight Ounce Coffee in Calgary, says it's easier than ever to manufacture it, thanks to advancements in technology.

Mainstream brands like Nescafé and Maxwell House make large amounts of instant coffee through a process called spray drying, which involves brewing coffee as strong as possible, then spraying that coffee into a heated chamber, creating the instant coffee powder.

But Hockin says a better quality coffee can be made by brewing the coffee then freeze-drying it instead. Years ago, the machine to do so would cost hundreds of thousands of dollars, and was as big as a shipping container.
Now, he says the machines cost about $3,000 to $4,000 Cdn, and can plug into the wall.
"It's not cheap to do, but it's certainly way less expensive than it would have been in the past," said Hockin.
Instant coffee jars sit on display in a Tesco supermarket on July 6, 2022 in Northwich, England. More specialty roasters are now offering their own take on instant coffee. (Getty Images)
Paying a premium

According to Robert Carter, it's not that people are replacing their at-home set up with instant coffee. Rather, Carter says, instant coffee is giving people another option to enjoy one of the most consumed drinks in Canada.
"We're not seeing a cannibalization taking place. We're seeing an expansion of the types of coffee products being consumed that are different than just your traditional brewed coffee.”
Starbucks VIA Ready Brew instant coffee is offered for sale at Starbucks coffee shop back in 2009. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)

And people are willing to pay a premium for that, says Hockin. He says it's the equivalent of buying a cup at a coffee shop, with some packets of four selling for $11, while some varieties sell for $42 for a six-pack.
But, he says, the quality is just as good, and it's as convenient as it gets.
"It's not their everyday cup of coffee, obviously. But they are very willing, very very willing to pay that money.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Philip Drost is a writer and editor for CBC Radio based in Fredericton. You can reach him at philip.drost@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Could this 93-year-old sprinter's muscles hold clues to healthy aging? Scientists think so
articles.summary: At 93, Italian sprinter Emma Mazzenga is giving scientists a rare look at just how much of the physical decline we associate with aging may not actually be inevitable.

image.caption: Emma Mazzenga, 93, poses for a photo in front of some of the dozens of medals she has won for running at her home in Padua, Italy. (Megan Williams/CBC)

blocks.text: At 93, Emma Maria Mazzenga still gets the jitters before a race.
"On race day, I'm very tense," she said. "People ask to interview me, and I tell them: Don't come near me until I've run."

Over the last four decades, Mazzenga has won 11 world titles, 31 European championships and 115 Italian races. She currently holds the 200-metre world record in the women's over-90 category: 50.33 seconds, set in 2024, when she was 91.
Now she is giving scientists a rare look at just how much of the physical decline we associate with aging may not actually be inevitable.

Mazzenga ran as a university student in Padua, in northern Italy. She then stopped for three decades while she taught high school biology and raised two children, largely on her own after her husband died.
In 1986, when she was 53, the president of her old university running club rounded up former athletes for the growing field of masters competitions, for those over age 35.
"One by one, my friends quit," she said. "I kept going."

In this 2024 file photo, a then-90-year-old Mazzenga shows her membership card for the Italian Athletics Federation, ahead of a race in San Biagio di Callalta, Italy. It shows her birthdate: Aug. 1, 1933. (Remo Casilli/Reuters)
She still trains three times a week, mostly short repeats of 50 to 200 metres. Slow jogging bores her.
What drives her isn't winning, Mazzenga said. In Italy, she has no rivals in her age category. "I come first because I have to. I'm the only one," she said. "I can't get any emotion out of that."
So she races the clock instead. "If I win with a mediocre time, it gives me no satisfaction."
Her proudest moment is still her first world title, the 400-metre W75 race at the World Masters Athletics Championships in Sacramento, Calif., won in 2011.
"There were just a handful of us Italians. I found myself alone on the podium," Mazzenga recalled.
Watch Emma Mazzenga, 93, compete in 100-metre race
From VO2 to muscle fibres
But eventually, her performances drew a different audience: Scientists.
Two years ago, Antonio La Torre, a scientist at the University of Milan and technical director of Italy’s athletic federation, tipped off two researchers who were studying how the body ages.

"We were told there was this woman who was able to run 200 metres in a very short time," said Martino Franchi, an associate professor of human physiology at the University of Padua. "But it was her age that we were really interested in."

items: 'Superagers' reveal how to stay sharp as you get older

blocks.text: Mazzegna became the most extreme case in a broader, two-year project called Trajector-Age, which tracked how muscles, nerves, heart and metabolism change in people over 50 to see whether exercise can slow decline.
Researchers from several Italian universities and the University of Wisconsin-Madison put Mazzenga through a gruelling cycling test and took biopsies from her thigh.
Mazzenga, then 90, competes in the 100-metre W90 category race in San Biagio di Callalta, Italy, on May 4, 2024. (Remo Casilli/Reuters)

Franchi says Mazzenga's maximal oxygen consumption is comparable to that of someone in their 50s. Also known as a VO2 max, it represents the greatest amount of oxygen a body can take in and use — a key measure of cardiovascular fitness.
"And she's 90," he said. "This is fantastic."

The bigger surprise was inside her muscles, said Franchi. Mazzenga has lost some of the fast-twitch fibres used for explosive movement, although fewer than expected. But her slow-twitch fibres — the ones that resist fatigue — are extraordinary.
"They are as big as a girl in her 20s," he said. "That's unique."
Martino Franchi gestures toward a screen showing a microscopic view of muscle fibres at his lab at the University of Padua, in Italy. (CBC)
Researchers think those unusually large fibres may help her hold her pace and compensate, at least partly, for the fast fibres lost with age.
Aging has happened, Franchi said, "but in a slower way." And so many years of training means that her body runs almost on auto-pilot when her feet hit the track.

The research was published earlier this year as two cases in the Journal of Applied Physiology, with a rendition of a Mazzenga landing on the cover. Lead scientist Marta Colosio received an award for the work at the American Physiology summit.
The team is now analyzing a second round of biopsies, along with genetic and molecular data, trying to tease apart what Mazzenga inherited versus what decades of training may have preserved.
Mazzenga walks with Martino Franchi, one of the researchers who has studied the 93-year-old's muscles and athletic performance to glean new insights into human aging. (CBC)

items: She just won 3 powerlifting medals. Oh, and she's 82 | The Moment

blocks.text: 'A bit of a rarity'
Mazzenga has her own theory. "I always say that if I had been sitting on the sofa, I would have aged differently."
With the running came fame — eventually. "No one paid much attention to me in my 80s, but after 90, yes," she jokes. "They look at me as a bit of a rarity."
She now speaks regularly at public events, most recently at la Repubblica's Festival di Salute, an annual health festival that draws Nobel laureates, scientists and sports champions.
As friends die and family members get busy with their own lives, Mazzenga says those connections — along with her masters teammates — matter almost as much as the training.
Mazzenga shows off her first pair of track shoes, when she first took to racing in her early 50s, at her home in Padua, Italy. (Megan Williams/CBC)
Franchi has his own reason for pushing exercise.
During the COVID-19 lockdowns, he noticed his father, then in his 70s, struggling to get up from the sofa. So Franchi printed out graphs linking inactivity to mortality.
"I said, 'Dad, I study sarcopenia. This is it,'" said Franchi, referring to the loss of muscle mass, strength and function with age. "He got scared, so he went back to the gym."
Today, Franchi's father can pull off full lunges and hikes several times a week.

items: Clara Hughes was used to pushing her body. When menopause hit, her body pushed back
Alberta woman, 61, breaks her own world record by planking for 5 hours

blocks.text: Franchi likes to tell the story to his students, telling them that physical activity is important — but be sure to keep doing it when you're older.
Asked what she'd tell someone 80, or even 90, thinking about taking up a sport, Mazzenga laughs. "You'd want to start a little earlier."
For those still able, she says, see a doctor, find a coach and match your body to the effort.
She herself has no plans to slow down. At a recent club final, she ran faster than she had two years earlier. "I was very pleased."
Mazzenga, centre, is seen in a photo with two fellow racers when she won the European Championship in 1998. (Megan Williams/CBC)

articles.title: Populist Czech PM Babis goes empty-handed in Senate elections
articles.summary: Opposition parties still control the Czech Senate, in a major blow to Prime Minister Andrej Babis' and his governing coalition.

image.caption: Babis has been described as 'Trumpist' in his outlookImage: Beata Zawrzel/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: The ruling coalition of populist billionaire Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis has failed to win a single seat in elections in the Senate.
The result means pro-Western opposition parties control the chamber, the upper house of parliament.

The election on Saturday was the first electoral test for Babis after he won parliamentary elections in October 2025 that returned him to power after a break of four years since his first term as premier.
What happened in the Czech Senate elections?

Final results from the two-day ballot showed that candidates directly linked to the opposition parties won 22 of the 27 seats up for grabs in the 81-member Senate, retaining a previous opposition majority.
The centrist ANO (or YES) movement led by Babis failed to win any more seats, leaving it with 14 Senate lawmakers.
Babis called the result "catastrophic."
"We certainly didn't expect that we wouldn't win a single Senate seat in this election," he said, but vowed to nonetheless go ahead with his government's agenda.
That includes an unpopular plan to revamp funding for the country’s public broadcasters.
Czech journalists warn of dangers of public media reform
His euroskeptic coalition has also ended direct military support for Ukraine as it defends itself against a Russian invasion, and opposed European Union policies to combat global warming.
Although the lower house of the Czech parliament plays the main legislative role, the Senate has a big say in passing constitutional amendments and approving Constitutional Court judges.

articles.title: An extraordinary life: descendant welcomes biography of woman ‘gifted’ to Queen Victoria
articles.summary:
A girl called Àìná was captured by an African king and later taken to England to become Sarah Forbes Bonetta, protege of the imperial monarch

When she was seven years old, Bayo Randle’s…

blocks.text: When she was seven years old, Bayo Randle’s great-great-grandmother Sarah Forbes Bonetta was presented to Queen Victoria at Windsor Castle as a “diplomatic gift” from an African king.
Victoria would go on to pay for Bonetta’s education, approve her marriage to one of west Africa’s wealthiest men, and become godmother to her eldest daughter.
But while Victoria took a genuine interest in Bonetta’s welfare, making the orphan a royal protege and meeting with her over the years, their relationship was part of a bigger agenda.
Now, as a biography is published – Becoming Sarah Forbes Bonetta: A Yorùbá Woman in Queen Victoria’s Court – Randle has spoken of his family history.

“I don’t think a human being, who has agency, could be ‘gifted’ from one to another, but had she not been gifted to Queen Victoria, would I be here today?” said Randle, a British-Nigerian barrister from London.

blocks.caption: Bayo Randle, Bonetta’s great-great-grandson, is a barrister in London. Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian

blocks.text: The new book, by a Canadian academic, Prof Henry Lovejoy, charts how Bonetta was brought to England by Frederick Forbes, of the Royal Navy’s West Africa Squadron, which was set up to enforce the abolition of the transatlantic trade.
Born in 1843 in Òkè-Òdàn, south-west Nigeria, Bonetta was originally called Àìná. Her family was killed in 1848 when her town was attacked by King Ghezo of Dahomey’s forces.
Bonetta, then five, is believed to have been captured by the agodjié – the all-female regiment depicted in the Hollywood movie The Woman King – and held at King Ghezo’s court.

blocks.caption: The book by Henry B Lovejoy. Photograph: supplied

blocks.text: In 1850, Forbes went to Dahomey – which is now Benin – to petition Ghezo to sign an anti-slavery treaty. The mission failed but Forbes asked Ghezo if he could take Bonetta to England.
Bonetta would go on to live a life of renown, becoming one of the most artistically represented and widely reported African women of her time. But she was never truly free.
Lovejoy’s book describes how, before Forbes arrived in England with her – giving her his own name and that of his ship, the Bonetta – he petitioned for her to be “the property of the crown”.

This meant Bonetta was “effectively indentured to Queen Victoria until age 19” under the post-abolition legal structures, Lovejoy said. Bonetta was then married off to James Pinson Labulo Davies, a merchant and philanthropist, of whom she would write: “I don’t feel a particle of love for him.”

Lovejoy’s research for the website liberatedafricans.org, developed with Kartikay Chadha, documents how, after abolition, more than 700,000 Africans “liberated” from enslavers were forced into indentures of up to 14 years “to pay for the cost of their own freedom” by governments including Britain’s.

Lovejoy claims Bonetta was at the elite end of this bonded labour system, “educated to be a missionary who would Christianise Africa”. In her lifetime her image was exploited as imperial iconography, promoting the idea that British colonialism of Africa was a “civilising mission”.

blocks.caption: Bonetta was a famous figure in 19th-century England. Photograph: Alamy

blocks.text: Lovejoy, of the University of Colorado Boulder, said: “Sarah’s imagery was used to project the idea of the queen’s benevolence – at a time when ‘liberated’ Africans are being forced into indentures.”

Nonetheless, when Bonetta attended the 1858 wedding of Queen Victoria’s daughter, the Princess Royal, American abolitionists saw it as proof that Victoria, then the most powerful woman on Earth, believed in equality.

For Randle, a plaster bust of Bonetta sculpted in 1851 by Benedetto Pistrucci, the Royal Mint’s chief engraver, symbolises the story’s “duality”. Randle saw it last year after Lovejoy had tracked it down to a private family collection in his research.

“Who gets to see what their great ancestor looked like as a child, the cultural markings on her face? That is amazing. But at the same time it was a bust prepared for phrenological purposes, within a racist framework, where [Bonetta] was shown as an ‘excellent specimen’,” Randle said.

Randle first learned his family history from his father, Adekunle Randle, a retired lawyer. The family still has the engraved goblet and plate that Queen Victoria gave to Bonetta’s daughter, Victoria, who, with the queen’s help, was educated at Cheltenham ladies’ college.
Lovejoy’s book challenges the myths that Bonetta was a Yoruba princess, that she herself was Queen Victoria’s goddaughter, and that she spent most of her life in England.

Randle, 37, who maintains his family’s ancestral ties with Òkè-Òdàn, welcomes research into Bonetta, who was a gifted linguist, musician, travel writer, educator and leading woman in 19th-century Lagos, until her death from tuberculosis in Madeira in 1880, aged 37.

“Whether [Lovejoy’s] book is comfortable for me is beside the point,” Randle said. “It’s for the advancement of knowledge and how we learn from the past. Where the real discomfort lies is in what [Bonetta] was the symbol of, what she was used for.

“But it would be a mistake to paint her story as entirely tragic,” he added. “My great-great-grandmother was very capable, courageous and dignified through adversity – through the trauma of losing her family, being displaced, and changing like a chameleon to fit into a culture so alien from what she’d known, she thrived. She is an early example of Black Britain.”

articles.title: Save-On-Foods loyalty program members had personal information accessed in cybersecurity breach
articles.summary: A major Canadian supermarket chain has notified customers in its loyalty program that their personal information was accessed during a cybersecurity breach. The chain says it discovered the activity…

image.caption: Save-On-Foods requires online shoppers to have a More Rewards profile, on top of anyone hoping to receive in-store discounts. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia

A major Canadian supermarket chain has notified customers in its loyalty program that their personal information was accessed during a cybersecurity breach. The chain says it discovered the activity on one of its servers, which was "quickly contained" before launching an investigation.
Names were accessed, possibly contact information and addresses, but no number on how many affected
A major Canadian supermarket chain has notified customers in its loyalty program that their personal information was accessed during a cybersecurity breach.

The Western Canadian grocery chain Save-On-Foods says it discovered unauthorized activity on one of its servers on Oct. 13, which was "quickly contained" before launching an investigation with a cybersecurity expert.
An email was then sent out to More Rewards customers Friday.
"We are writing to let you know about an incident involving your personal information," the email read.
Customers who received an email were told that their names and — if provided — addresses, phone numbers, email addresses and dates of birth were accessed.
CBC News asked Save-On-Foods how many customers were affected in the data breach but did not receive a number by deadline.
Save-On-Foods requires online shoppers to be signed up for the More Rewards program, which also offers members exclusive in-store discounts.
The email said "based on the information available," no other personal information, such as credit card data or passwords, was accessed.
Phishing concerns

However, the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security says personal information can be used by cybercriminals to make phishing attacks more convincing, impersonating trusted organizations to trick people into sharing sensitive information or sending money.
"Most of these break-ins are opportunistic," wrote Richard Frank, director of Simon Fraser University’s international cybercrime centre, in an email to CBC News.
He said criminals often gain access to corporate networks through employees accidentally clicking malicious links or downloading malware.
But that’s when criminals can "map the network," identify whatever they can steal to monetize, "and loyalty programs usually provide enough details to make realistic scams."

Frank explained that personal information is often used by cybercriminals to impersonate companies in emails requesting more information or containing malicious links, potentially allowing them to steal identities, banking information or credit card details.
He said criminals can use that more sensitive information to make fraudulent purchases through online stores and even cryptomarkets.
Community response

Numerous Reddit commenters on B.C. and Alberta sub-communities expressed frustration with discount systems that require customers to provide personal information through loyalty programs, arguing data like that can be sold corporately and makes them a target for cybercrime.
Several of those subreddit posts suggest that customers who received the notification and then tried to change their passwords were met with a recurring error.

More Rewards members are being told to be vigilant about suspicious calls or messages, as Save-On-Foods says it will not send any communications asking for passwords, banking information, payment information, social insurance numbers or security question answers.
In an email to CBC News, Save-On-Foods said it notified the appropriate authorities and privacy regulators.
CBC News reached out to the Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner for B.C. to confirm whether it had been notified of the incident but did not hear back before publication.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Arden McLeod, from Vancouver, is an associate producer with CBC News. He has a passion for community storytelling, local news, and reflecting the values of B.C. He graduated from the British Columbia Institute of Technology's broadcast and online journalism program. You can reach him at Arden.McLeod@cbc.ca.
